\Omega = (\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{C}, \mathfrak{F}, \mathfrak{G}, \mathfrak{H} \hspace{-2pt} fa', b', c', 2f', 2g', 2h'),
\]
and putting
\begin{align*}
E_\Phi &= (\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa', \ldots) \quad (= \partial_x\Omega_g), \\
F_\Phi &= (\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\mathfrak{d}a', \ldots) \quad (= \partial_x\Omega_p),
\end{align*}
we have, post, Nos.\ 41 to 46,
\begin{align*}
-2(m - 1)(m - 2)F_\Phi + (3m - 7)^2E_\Phi &= (3m - 6)(3m - 7)H\Omega_g, \\
(m - 1)(3m - 8)F_\Psi + (3m - 7)(3m - 8)F_\Psi - (m - 1)^2E_\Psi &= (3m - 6)(3m - 7)H\Omega_p, \\
-(m - 1)F_\Psi + (3m - 7)F_\Psi &= (3m - 7)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H,
\end{align*}
and the foregoing equation becomes
\begin{multline*}
(3m - 7)\mathcal{R} = -(5m^2 - 18m + 17)(3m - 6)(3m - 7)H\Omega_g \\
- (5m - 9)(m - 2)(3m - 6)(3m - 7)H\Omega_p \\
+ (m - 2)(25m^2 - 103m + 106)(3m - 7)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\begin{art}
But we have
\begin{align*}
\frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, H, \Omega_g) - (3m - 6)H\Omega_g + (2m - 4)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H &= 0, \tag{J} \\
\frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, H, \Omega_p) - (3m - 6)H\Omega_p + (3m - 6)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H &= 0, \tag{J}
\end{align*}
that is
\begin{align*}
3(m - 2)H\Omega_g &= 2(m - 2)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H + \frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, H, \Omega_g), \\
3(m - 2)H\Omega_p &= (3m - 8)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H + \frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, H, \Omega_p),
\end{align*}
and we thus obtain
\begin{multline*}
\mathcal{R} = -(5m^2 - 18m + 17)\{2(m - 2)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H + \frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, H, \Omega_g)\} \\
- (5m - 9)(m - 2)\{(3m - 8)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H + \frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, H, \Omega_p)\} \\
+ (25m^2 - 103m + 106)(m - 2)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H,
\end{multline*}
where the coefficient of $(m - 2)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H$ is
\begin{align*}
&-(10m^2 - 36m + 34) \\
&-(5m - 9)(3m - 8) \\
&+ (25m^2 - 103m + 106),
\end{align*}
which is $= 0$. Hence
\[
\mathcal{R} = -(5m^2 - 18m + 17)\frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, H, \Omega_g) - (5m - 9)(m - 2)\frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, H, \Omega_p).
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Substituting this in the equation
\[
3\mathcal{R} + (m - 2)^2\{-27H\Jac(U, H, \Omega) + 40\Jac(U, \mathcal{W}, H)\} = 0,
\]
the result contains the factor $\Psi$, and, throwing this out, the condition is
\begin{multline*}
3H\{-(5m^2 - 18m + 17)\Jac(U, H, \Omega_g) - (5m - 9)(m - 2)\Jac(U, H, \Omega_p)\} \\
+ (m - 2)^2\{27H^2\Jac(U, H, \Omega) - 40\Jac(U, \mathcal{W}, H)\} = 0,
\end{multline*}
or, as this may also be written,
\begin{multline*}
-(15m^2 - 54m + 51)H\Jac(U, H, \Omega_g) - 3(5m - 9)(m - 2)H\Jac(U, H, \Omega_p) \\
+ 27(m - 2)^2\{H\Jac(U, H, \Omega_g) + H\Jac(U, H, \Omega_p)\} \\
- 40(m - 2)^2\Jac(U, \mathcal{W}, H) = 0.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Hence the condition finally is
\begin{multline*}
(12m^2 - 54m + 57)H\Jac(U, H, \Omega_g) + (m - 2)(12m - 27)H\Jac(U, H, \Omega_p) \\
- 40(m - 2)^2\Jac(U, \mathcal{W}, H) = 0,
\end{multline*}
or, as this may also be written,
\begin{multline*}
-3(m - 1)H\Jac(U, H, \Omega_g) + (m - 2)(12m - 27)H\Jac(U, H, \Omega) \\
- 40(m - 2)^2\Jac(U, \mathcal{W}, H) = 0,
\end{multline*}
viz.\ the sextactic points are the intersections of the curve $m$ with the curve represented by this equation; and observing that $U$, $H$, $\Omega H$, and $\Psi$ are of the orders $m$, $3m - 6$, $8m - 18$ respectively, the order of the curve is as above mentioned $= 12m - 27$.
\end{art}

\subsection*{Article Nos.\ 28 to 30.---Application to a Cubic.}

\begin{art}
I have in my former memoir, No.~30, shown that for a cubic curve
\[
\Omega = (\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{C}, \mathfrak{F}, \mathfrak{G}, \mathfrak{H} \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2 \Phi = -2\Psi \cdot U = 0;
\]
this implies $\Jac(U, H, \Omega) = 0$, and hence if one of the two Jacobians, $\Jac(U, H, \Omega_g)$, $\Jac(U, H, \Omega_p)$ vanish, the other will also vanish. Now, using the canonical form
\[
U = x^3 + y^3 + z^3 + 6lxyz = 0,
\]
we have
\begin{align*}
\Omega &= (\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa', \ldots) \\
&= (yz - l^2x^2, \; zx - l^2y^2, \; xy - l^2z^2, \; l^2yz - lx^2, \; l^2zx - ly^2, \; l^2xy - lz^2) \\
&\quad (\mathfrak{A}', \mathfrak{B}', \mathfrak{C}', \mathfrak{F}', \mathfrak{G}', \mathfrak{H}' \hspace{-2pt} fa, b, c, 2f, 2g, 2h) \\
&= (-3l^2x, \; -3l^2y, \; -3l^2z, \; (1 + 2l^3)x, \; (1 + 2l^3)y, \; (1 + 2l^3)z),
\end{align*}
the development of which in fact gives the last-mentioned result. But applying this formula to the calculation of $\Jac(U, H, \Omega_g)$, then disregarding numerical factors, we have
\begin{align*}
\partial_x\Omega_g &= (yz - l^2x^2, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_xa', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f-3l^2, 0, 0, (1 + 2l^3), 0, 0) \\
&= -3l^2(yz - l^2x^2) + (1 + 2l^3)(yz - lx^2) \\
&= (-l + l^4)(x^2 + 2lyz) = 3\partial_x U;
\end{align*}
and in like manner $\partial_y\Omega_g = 3\partial_y U$, $\partial_z\Omega_g = 3\partial_z U$, and therefore
\[
\Jac(U, H, \Omega_g) = 3\Jac(U, H, U) = 0,
\]
whence also
\[
\Jac(U, H, \Omega_p) = 0;
\]
and the condition for a sextactic point assumes the more simple form,
\[
\Jac(U, H, \Psi) = 0.
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Now (former memoir, No.~32) we have
\begin{align*}
\Psi &= (\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{C}, \mathfrak{F}, \mathfrak{G}, \mathfrak{H} \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2 \Phi \\
&= (1 + 8l^3)^2(x^6 + y^6 + z^6) \\
&\quad + (-9l^2)(x^3 + y^3 + z^3)^2 \\
&\quad + (-2l - 5l^4 - 20l^7)(x^3 + y^3 + z^3)xyz \\
&\quad + (-15l^3 - 78l^6 + 12l^9)x^2y^2z^2,
\end{align*}
or observing that $x^3 + y^3 + z^3$ and $xyz$, and therefore the last three lines of the expression of $\Psi$ are functions of $U$ ($= x^3 + y^3 + z^3 + 6lxyz$) and $H$ ($= -l^2(x^3 + y^3 + z^3) + (1 + 2l^3)xyz$), and consequently give rise to the term $= 0$ in $\Jac(U, H, \Psi)$, we may write
\[
\Psi = (1 + 8l^3)^2(x^6 + y^6 + z^6).
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
We have then, disregarding a constant factor,
\[
\Jac(U, H, \Psi) = \Jac(x^3 + y^3 + z^3, \; xyz, \; x^6 + y^6 + z^6),
\]
\[
= \begin{vmatrix}
x^2 & y^2 & z^2 \\
yz & zx & xy \\
x^5 & y^5 & z^5
\end{vmatrix}
\]
\begin{align*}
&= x^7(y^4 - z^4) + y^7(z^4 - x^4) + z^7(x^4 - y^4), \\
&\propto (y^2 - z^2)(z^2 - x^2)(x^2 - y^2),
\end{align*}
so that the sextactic points are the intersections of the curve
\[
U = x^3 + y^3 + z^3 + 6lxyz = 0,
\]
with the curve
\[
(y^2 - z^2)(z^2 - x^2)(x^2 - y^2) = 0.
\]
\end{art}

\subsection*{Article Nos.\ 31 to 33.---Proof of identities for the first transformation.}

\begin{art}
\textit{Calculation of} $(\mathfrak{d}_1^5 + 10\mathfrak{d}_1^3\mathfrak{d}_2 + 10\mathfrak{d}_1^2\mathfrak{d}_3 + 15\mathfrak{d}_1\mathfrak{d}_2^2)U$.

Writing $\mathfrak{d}$ in place of $D$, we have (former memoir, No.~20)
\[
\mathfrak{d}_1^2 U = \frac{1}{(m - 1)^2}\{-3(m - 2)H\Phi + (m - 1)\Phi\mathfrak{d}_1 H\}.
\]
But
\[
\mathfrak{d}_1^2 U = \frac{1}{(m - 1)^2}\{-(3m - 6)H\Phi + \Phi\mathfrak{d}_1 H\} \quad \text{[former memoir, Nos.\ 21 and 22]},
\]
and thence
\[
(\mathfrak{d}_1^3 + 6\mathfrak{d}_1\mathfrak{d}_2)U = \frac{1}{(m - 1)^3}\{(18m^2 - 66m + 60)H^2\Phi + \ldots\},
\]
whence operating on each side with $\mathfrak{d}_1$, $= \mathfrak{d}$,
\begin{multline*}
(\mathfrak{d}_1^5 + 10\mathfrak{d}_1^3\mathfrak{d}_2 + 6\mathfrak{d}_1^2\mathfrak{d}_3 + 12\mathfrak{d}_1\mathfrak{d}_2^2)U \\
= \frac{1}{(m - 1)^4}\{(18m^2 - 66m + 60)H^2\mathfrak{d}_1\Phi + \ldots\} \\
+ \frac{1}{(m - 1)^4}\{(-10m + 18)(\mathfrak{d}.\nabla)\Phi + \mathfrak{d}\nabla\Phi\}.
\end{multline*}
We have besides (see Appendix, Nos.\ 69 to 74),
\[
\mathfrak{d}_1\mathfrak{d}_3 U = \ldots
\]
and thence
\begin{multline*}
(4\mathfrak{d}_1\mathfrak{d}_2^2 + 3\mathfrak{d}_1^2\mathfrak{d}_3)U = \frac{1}{(m - 1)^4}\{(9m^2 - 21)m + (-9m^2 + 9)\Phi H\} \\
+ \ldots
\end{multline*}
and adding this to the foregoing expression for $(\mathfrak{d}_1^5 + 10\mathfrak{d}_1^3\mathfrak{d}_2 + 6\mathfrak{d}_1^2\mathfrak{d}_3 + 12\mathfrak{d}_1\mathfrak{d}_2^2)U$, we have
\begin{multline*}
(\mathfrak{d}_1^5 + 10\mathfrak{d}_1^3\mathfrak{d}_2 + 10\mathfrak{d}_1^2\mathfrak{d}_3 + 15\mathfrak{d}_1\mathfrak{d}_2^2)U = \\
\frac{\Phi}{(m - 1)^4}\{(27m^2 - 96m + 81)H\mathfrak{d}_1^4 + (17m^2 - 56m + 51)\Phi\mathfrak{d}_1 H\} \\
+ \frac{\Psi}{(m - 1)^4}\{(-14m + 22)(\mathfrak{d}.\nabla)H + (-10m + 18)\mathfrak{d}\nabla H\} \\
+ \frac{\Omega}{(m - 1)^4}\{9\Omega\}.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\begin{art}
\textit{Calculation of} $\mathfrak{d}_1 U\mathfrak{d}_4 H + 2\mathfrak{d}_1^2 U\mathfrak{d}_3 H + 2\mathfrak{d}_1^3 U\mathfrak{d}_2 H$.

We have
\begin{align*}
\mathfrak{d}_1 U &= \frac{m - 1}{(m - 1)^2}\mathfrak{d}_1 U, & \mathfrak{d}_2 H &= \mathfrak{d}_1 H, \\
\mathfrak{d}_1^2 U &= \frac{(m - 1)^2}{(m - 1)^3}\mathfrak{d}_1^2 U, & \mathfrak{d}_3 H &= \mathfrak{d}_1 H, \\
\mathfrak{d}_1^3 U &= \frac{(m - 1)^3}{(m - 1)^4}\mathfrak{d}_1^3 U, & \mathfrak{d}_4 H &= \frac{m - 1}{(m - 1)}(-3m + 6)H\Phi - \Phi\mathfrak{d}_1 H + \frac{1}{m - 1}(\mathfrak{d}.\nabla)H;
\end{align*}
for which values see Appendix, No.~58. And hence the expression sought for is
\begin{multline*}
\ldots \\
+ 2(m - 1)\Phi^2\mathfrak{d}_1 H \\
+ 2H\{(-3m + 6)H\Phi - \Phi\mathfrak{d}_1 H + \frac{1}{m - 1}(\mathfrak{d}.\nabla)H\}\Phi,
\end{multline*}
which is
\begin{multline*}
\ldots \\
+ (m - 1)\mathfrak{d}_1 H\Phi^2 H \\
+ (-6m + 12)H^2\Phi^2 - 3H\Phi^2\mathfrak{d}_1 H\} \\
+ (m - 1)^2\{2H(\mathfrak{d}.\nabla)H - \mathfrak{d}H\nabla H\}.
\end{multline*}

But we have, former memoir, Nos.\ 21 and 25,
\begin{align*}
\mathfrak{d}_1^2 H &= \ldots, \\
\mathfrak{d}_1^3 H &= \frac{(3m - 6)(3m - 7)}{(m - 1)^2}H^2\Phi + \frac{6m - 14}{(m - 1)^2}\Phi\mathfrak{d}_1 H + \ldots,
\end{align*}
so that the foregoing expression becomes
\begin{multline*}
\frac{1}{(m - 1)^2}\{-(8m - 16)H^2\mathfrak{d}_1 H + \Phi\mathfrak{d}H\nabla H\} \\
- \frac{(3m - 6)(3m - 7)}{(m - 1)^2}\Phi H\mathfrak{d}_1 H - \frac{6m - 14}{(m - 1)^2}\Phi^2\mathfrak{d}_1 H \\
+ \frac{1}{(m - 1)^2}\{3H^2\mathfrak{d}_1 H - (16m - 12)H^2\mathfrak{d}_1 H\} \\
+ \frac{1}{(m - 1)^2}\{2H(\mathfrak{d}.\nabla)H - \mathfrak{d}H\nabla H\};
\end{multline*}
or finally
\begin{multline*}
\mathfrak{d}_1 U\mathfrak{d}_4 H + 2\mathfrak{d}_1^2 U\mathfrak{d}_3 H + 2\mathfrak{d}_1^3 U\mathfrak{d}_2 H = \\
\frac{1}{(m - 1)^2}\{(-6m^2 + 18m - 12)H\mathfrak{d}_1^4 + (-17m^2 + 60m - 55)H^2\Phi\mathfrak{d}_1 H\} \\
+ \frac{1}{(m - 1)^3}\{(2m - 2)H(\mathfrak{d}.\nabla)H + (8m - 16)\mathfrak{d}H\nabla H\} \\
+ \frac{1}{(m - 1)^4}\{9\Omega\}.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\begin{art}
\textit{Calculation of} $\mathfrak{d}_1^3 U\mathfrak{d}_1^2 U$.

This is
\[
\frac{1}{(m - 1)^4}H\mathfrak{d}_1 H \cdot \Phi^2 H = \ldots
\]
\end{art}

\subsection*{Article Nos.\ 34 and 35.---The Jacobian Formula.}

\begin{art}
In general, if $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ be functions of the degrees $p$, $q$, $r$, $s$ respectively, we have identically
\[
\begin{vmatrix}
pP & qQ & rR & sS \\
\partial_x P & \partial_x Q & \partial_x R & \partial_x S \\
\partial_y P & \partial_y Q & \partial_y R & \partial_y S \\
\partial_z P & \partial_z Q & \partial_z R & \partial_z S
\end{vmatrix} = 0,
\]
or, what is the same thing,
\[
pP \Jac(Q, R, S) - qQ \Jac(R, S, P) + rR \Jac(S, P, Q) - sS \Jac(P, Q, R) = 0.
\]

Hence in particular if $P = U$, and assuming $U = 0$, we have
\[
-qQ \Jac(R, S, U) + rR \Jac(S, U, Q) - sS \Jac(U, Q, R) = 0.
\]

If moreover $Q = \Phi$, and therefore $q = 1$, we have
\[
-\Phi \Jac(R, S, U) + rR \Jac(S, U, \Phi) - sS \Jac(U, \Phi, R) = 0;
\]
or, as this may also be written,
\[
-\frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, R, S) + rR \Jac(U, \Phi, S) - sS \Jac(U, \Phi, R) = 0;
\]
that is
\[
-\frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, R, S) + rR\mathfrak{d}S - sS\mathfrak{d}R = 0.
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Particular cases are
\begin{align*}
(2m - 4)\Phi\mathfrak{d}_1 H - (3m - 6)H\mathfrak{d}_1\Phi &= \frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, \Phi, H), \quad \text{ante, No.~12}, \\
(5m - 11)\nabla H\mathfrak{d}_1 H - (3m - 6)H\mathfrak{d}_1(\nabla H) &= \frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, \nabla H, H), \\
(2m - 4)\nabla \mathfrak{d}_1\Phi - (3m - 6)\Phi\mathfrak{d}_1\nabla &= \frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, \nabla, H), \\
(5m - 12)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H - (3m - 6)H\mathfrak{d}_1\Omega &= \frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, \Omega, H), \\
(8m - 18)\mathcal{W}\mathfrak{d}_1 H - (3m - 6)H\mathfrak{d}_1\mathcal{W} &= \frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, \mathcal{W}, H), \\
(2m - 4)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H - (3m - 6)H\Omega_g &= \frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, \Omega, H), \\
(3m - 8)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H - (3m - 6)H\Omega_p &= \frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, \Omega_p, H),
\end{align*}
where it is to be observed that in the third of these formul\ae\ I have, in accordance with the notation before employed, written $\mathfrak{d}.\nabla$ to denote the result of the operation $\mathfrak{d}$ performed on $\nabla$ as operand. I have also written $\nabla : \mathfrak{d}H$ to show that the operation $\nabla$ is not to be performed on the following $\mathfrak{d}H$ as an operand, but that it remains as an unperformed operation. As regards the last two equations, it is to be remarked that the demonstration in the last preceding number depends merely on the homogeneity of the functions, and the orders of these functions: in the former of the two formul\ae, the differentiation of $\Omega$ is performed upon $\Omega$ in regard to the coordinates $(x, y, z)$ in so far only as they enter through $U$, and $\Omega$ is therefore to be regarded as a function of the order $2m - 4$; in the latter of the two formul\ae\ the differentiation is to be performed in regard to the coordinates in so far only as they enter through $H$, and $\Omega$ is therefore to be regarded as a function of the order $3m - 8$. The two formul\ae\ might also be written
\begin{align*}
(2m - 4)\nabla\mathfrak{d}_1 H - (3m - 6)H\Omega_g &= \frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, \Omega_g, H), \\
(3m - 8)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H - (3m - 6)H\Omega_p &= \frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, \Omega_p, H);
\end{align*}
and it may be noticed that, adding these together, we obtain the foregoing formula,
\[
(5m - 12)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H - (3m - 6)H\mathfrak{d}_1\Omega = \frac{\Psi}{m - 1}\Jac(U, \Omega, H).
\]
\end{art}

\subsection*{Article Nos.\ 36 to 40.---Proof of equation $(\mathfrak{d}.\nabla)H = \Jac(U, H, \Phi)$, used in the second transformation.}

\begin{art}
We have
\begin{align*}
\nabla &= (\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z) \\
&= (\mathfrak{A}\partial_x + \mathfrak{F}\partial_y + \mathfrak{G}\partial_z, \; \mathfrak{F}\partial_x + \mathfrak{B}\partial_y + \mathfrak{H}\partial_z, \; \mathfrak{G}\partial_x + \mathfrak{H}\partial_y + \mathfrak{C}\partial_z \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu).
\end{align*}
Also
\begin{align*}
\mathfrak{d} &= (Bv - C\mu)\partial_x + (C\lambda - A\nu)\partial_y + (A\mu - B\lambda)\partial_z \\
&= \lambda P + \mu Q + \nu R,
\end{align*}
if for a moment $P, Q, R = C\partial_y - B\partial_z$, $A\partial_z - C\partial_x$, $B\partial_x - A\partial_y$.

Hence
\[
\mathfrak{d}.\nabla = (P\lambda + Q\mu + R\nu) \cdot (\mathfrak{A}\partial_x + \mathfrak{F}\partial_y + \mathfrak{G}\partial_z, \; \mathfrak{F}\partial_x + \mathfrak{B}\partial_y + \mathfrak{H}\partial_z, \; \mathfrak{G}\partial_x + \mathfrak{H}\partial_y + \mathfrak{C}\partial_z \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu),
\]
viz.\ coefficient of $\lambda^2$
\[
= P\mathfrak{A}\partial_x + P\mathfrak{F}\partial_y + P\mathfrak{G}\partial_z
\]
and so for the other terms; whence also in $(\mathfrak{d}.\nabla)H$ the coefficients of $\lambda^2$, \&c.\ are
\[
(P\mathfrak{A}\partial_x + P\mathfrak{F}\partial_y + P\mathfrak{G}\partial_z)H, \text{ \&c.}
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Again, in $\Jac(U, H, \Phi)$, where $\Phi = (\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{C}, \mathfrak{F}, \mathfrak{G}, \mathfrak{H} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu)^2$, the coefficients of $\lambda^2$, \&c.\ are $\Jac(U, H, \mathfrak{A})$, \&c.; and hence the assumed equation
\[
(\mathfrak{d}.\nabla)H = \Jac(U, H, \Phi),
\]
in regard to the term in $\lambda^2$, is
\[
(P\mathfrak{A}\partial_x + P\mathfrak{F}\partial_y + P\mathfrak{G}\partial_z)H = \Jac(U, H, \mathfrak{A}),
\]
and we have
\begin{align*}
\Jac(U, H, \mathfrak{A}) &= \begin{vmatrix} A & B & C \\ \partial_x H & \partial_y H & \partial_z H \\ \partial_x\mathfrak{A} & \partial_y\mathfrak{A} & \partial_z\mathfrak{A} \end{vmatrix} \\
&= \{\partial_x H(C\partial_y - B\partial_z) + \partial_y H(A\partial_z - C\partial_x) + \partial_z H(B\partial_x - A\partial_y)\}\mathfrak{A} \\
&= (\partial_x H \cdot P + \partial_y H \cdot Q + \partial_z H \cdot R)\mathfrak{A};
\end{align*}
so that the equation is
\[
P\mathfrak{A}\partial_x H + P\mathfrak{F}\partial_y H + P\mathfrak{G}\partial_z H = P\mathfrak{A}\partial_x H + Q\mathfrak{A}\partial_y H + R\mathfrak{A}\partial_z H,
\]
or, as this may be written,
\begin{multline*}
[(B\partial_z - C\partial_y)\mathfrak{F} - (C\partial_x - A\partial_z)\mathfrak{A}]\partial_y H \\
+ [(B\partial_z - C\partial_y)\mathfrak{G} - (A\partial_y - B\partial_x)\mathfrak{A}]\partial_z H = 0.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\begin{art}
The coefficient of $\partial_y H$ is
\[
B(\partial_z\mathfrak{F} - \partial_y\mathfrak{A}) + C(\partial_x\mathfrak{A} - \partial_z\mathfrak{F}) + A(\partial_y\mathfrak{F} - \partial_x\mathfrak{G}),
\]
which, in virtue of the identity, post, No.~40, $\partial_x\mathfrak{A} + \partial_y\mathfrak{F} + \partial_z\mathfrak{G} = 0$,
\[
= A\partial_x\mathfrak{A} + B\partial_y\mathfrak{F} + C\partial_z\mathfrak{G};
\]
and in like manner the coefficient of $\partial_z H$ is
\[
= -(A\partial_x\mathfrak{G} + B\partial_y\mathfrak{B} + C\partial_z\mathfrak{H}),
\]
so that the equation is
\[
(A\partial_x\mathfrak{A} + B\partial_y\mathfrak{F} + C\partial_z\mathfrak{G})\partial_y H - (A\partial_x\mathfrak{G} + B\partial_y\mathfrak{B} + C\partial_z\mathfrak{H})\partial_z H = 0.
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
But we have
\begin{align*}
\mathfrak{A}a + \mathfrak{F}h + \mathfrak{G}g &= H, \\
\mathfrak{A}h + \mathfrak{F}b + \mathfrak{G}f &= 0, \\
\mathfrak{A}g + \mathfrak{F}f + \mathfrak{G}c &= 0,
\end{align*}
or multiplying by $x$, $y$, $z$ and adding,
\[
(m - 1)(\mathfrak{A}A + \mathfrak{F}B + \mathfrak{G}C) = xH;
\]
whence also
\[
(m - 1)(\mathfrak{A}\partial_x A + \mathfrak{F}\partial_x B + \mathfrak{G}\partial_x C + A\partial_x\mathfrak{A} + B\partial_x\mathfrak{F} + C\partial_x\mathfrak{G}) = x\partial_x H + H,
\]
that is
\[
(m - 1)(A\partial_x\mathfrak{A} + B\partial_x\mathfrak{F} + C\partial_x\mathfrak{G}) = x\partial_x H;
\]
and in like manner
\[
(m - 1)(A\partial_y\mathfrak{A} + B\partial_y\mathfrak{F} + C\partial_y\mathfrak{G}) = x\partial_y H,
\]
whence the equation in question. The terms in $\lambda^2$ are thus shown to be equal, and it might in a similar manner be shown that the terms in $\mu\nu$ are equal; the other terms will then be equal, and we have therefore
\[
(\mathfrak{d}.\nabla)H = \Jac(U, H, \Phi).
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
The identity
\[
\partial_x\mathfrak{A} + \partial_y\mathfrak{F} + \partial_z\mathfrak{G} = 0
\]
assumed in the course of the foregoing proof is easily proved. We have in fact
\begin{align*}
\partial_x\mathfrak{A} + \partial_y\mathfrak{F} + \partial_z\mathfrak{G} &= \partial_x(bc - f^2) + \partial_y(fg - ch) + \partial_z(fh - bg) \\
&= b(\partial_x c - \partial_y f) + c(\partial_x b - \partial_z g) + f(-2\partial_x f + \partial_y g + \partial_z h) \\
&\quad + g(\partial_y f - \partial_z b) + h(-\partial_y c + \partial_z f),
\end{align*}
where the coefficients of $b$, $c$, $f$, $g$, $h$ separately vanish: we have of course the system
\begin{align*}
\partial_x\mathfrak{A} + \partial_y\mathfrak{F} + \partial_z\mathfrak{G} &= 0, \\
\partial_x\mathfrak{F} + \partial_y\mathfrak{B} + \partial_z\mathfrak{H} &= 0, \\
\partial_x\mathfrak{G} + \partial_y\mathfrak{H} + \partial_z\mathfrak{C} &= 0.
\end{align*}
\end{art}

\subsection*{Article Nos.\ 41 to 46.---Proof of identities for the fourth transformation.}

\begin{art}
Consider the coefficients $(a, b, c, f, g, h)$ and the inverse set $(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{C}, \mathfrak{F}, \mathfrak{G}, \mathfrak{H})$, and the coefficients $(a', b', c', f', g', h')$, and the inverse set $(\mathfrak{A}', \mathfrak{B}', \mathfrak{C}', \mathfrak{F}', \mathfrak{G}', \mathfrak{H}')$; then we have identically
\begin{multline*}
(a, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fx, y, z)^2(\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa, \ldots) - (\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fax + hy + gz, \ldots)^2 \\
= (a', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fx, y, z)^2(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa', \ldots) - (\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa'x + h'y + g'z, \ldots)^2,
\end{multline*}
where $(\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa, \ldots)$ and $(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa', \ldots)$ stand for
\[
(\mathfrak{A}', \mathfrak{B}', \mathfrak{C}', \mathfrak{F}', \mathfrak{G}', \mathfrak{H}' \hspace{-2pt} fa, b, c, 2f, 2g, 2h)
\]
and
\[
(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{C}, \mathfrak{F}, \mathfrak{G}, \mathfrak{H} \hspace{-2pt} fa', b', c', 2f', 2g', 2h')
\]
respectively.
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Taking $(a, b, c, f, g, h)$, the second differential coefficients of a function $U$ of the order $m$, and in like manner $(a', b', c', f', g', h')$, the second differential coefficients of a function $U'$ of the order $m'$, we have
\begin{multline*}
m(m - 1)U \cdot (\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2 U' - (m - 1)^2(\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x U', \partial_y U', \partial_z U')^2 \\
= m'(m' - 1)U' \cdot (\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2 U - (m' - 1)^2(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x U, \partial_y U, \partial_z U)^2;
\end{multline*}
and in particular if $U'$ be the Hessian of $U$, then $m' = 3m - 6$.
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Hence writing
\[
\Omega = (\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2 H, \quad \nabla_1 = (\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x H, \partial_y H, \partial_z H)^2,
\]
we have
\[
\Omega_1 = (\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2 U, \quad \nabla_1 = (\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x U, \partial_y U, \partial_z U)^2;
\]
\[
m(m - 1)U\Omega_1 - (m - 1)^2\nabla_1 = (3m - 6)(3m - 7)H\Omega - (3m - 7)^2\nabla;
\]
or if $U = 0$, then
\[
-(m - 1)^2\nabla_1 = (3m - 6)(3m - 7)H\Omega - (3m - 7)^2\nabla;
\]
whence also
\[
-(m - 1)^2\mathfrak{d}_x\nabla_1 = (3m - 6)(3m - 7)\{H\mathfrak{d}_x\Omega + \Omega\mathfrak{d}_x H\} - (3m - 7)^2\mathfrak{d}_x\nabla,
\]
which is the formula, ante No.~21.
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Recurring to the original formula, since this is an actual identity, we may operate on it with the differential symbol $\mathfrak{d}$ on the three assumptions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item $(a, b, c, f, g, h)$, $(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{C}, \mathfrak{F}, \mathfrak{G}, \mathfrak{H})$ are alone variable.
\item $(a', b', c', f', g', h')$, $(\mathfrak{A}', \mathfrak{B}', \mathfrak{C}', \mathfrak{F}', \mathfrak{G}', \mathfrak{H}')$ are alone variable.
\item $(x, y, z)$ are alone variable.
\end{enumerate}
We thus obtain
\begin{multline*}
(a, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fx, y, z)^2(\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa, \ldots) = (a', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fx, y, z)^2(\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa', \ldots) \\
- 2(\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fax + hy + gz, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa\mathfrak{d}x + y\mathfrak{d}b + z\mathfrak{d}c, \ldots),
\end{multline*}
\begin{multline*}
(a, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fx, y, z)^2(\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa, \ldots) = (\mathfrak{d}a', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fx, y, z)^2(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa', \ldots) \\
- (\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fax + hy + gz, \ldots)^2 + (a', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fx, y, z)^2(\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa', \ldots) \\
- 2(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa'x + h'y + g'z, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fx\mathfrak{d}a' + y\mathfrak{d}h' + z\mathfrak{d}g', \ldots),
\end{multline*}
\begin{multline*}
2(a, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fx, y, z \hspace{-2pt} f\mathfrak{d}x, \mathfrak{d}y, \mathfrak{d}z)(\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa, \ldots) = 2(a', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fx, y, z \hspace{-2pt} f\mathfrak{d}x, \mathfrak{d}y, \mathfrak{d}z)(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa', \ldots) \\
- 2(\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fax + hy + gz, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa\mathfrak{d}x + h\mathfrak{d}y + g\mathfrak{d}z, \ldots) \\
- 2(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa'x + h'y + g'z, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa'\mathfrak{d}x + h'\mathfrak{d}y + g'\mathfrak{d}z, \ldots).
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\begin{art}
If in these equations respectively we suppose as before that $(a, b, c, f, g, h)$ are the second differential coefficients of a function $U$ of the order $m$, and $(a', b', c', f', g', h')$ the second differential coefficients of a function $V$ of the order $m'$; and that $(A, B, C)$, $(A', B', C')$ are the first differential coefficients of these functions respectively, then after some easy reductions we have
\begin{multline*}
(m - 1)(m - 2)\mathfrak{d}U(\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa, \ldots) = m'(m' - 1)V'(a\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa', \ldots) \\
+ m(m - 1)U(\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\mathfrak{d}a, \ldots) - (m' - 1)^2(\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA', B', C')^2 \\
- 2(m - 1)(m - 2)(\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C \hspace{-2pt} f\mathfrak{d}A, \mathfrak{d}B, \mathfrak{d}C),
\end{multline*}
\begin{multline*}
m(m - 1)U(\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa', \ldots) = (m' - 1)(m' - 2)\mathfrak{d}U'(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa', \ldots) \\
- (m' - 1)^2(\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C)^2 + m'(m' - 1)V'(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa\mathfrak{d}a', \ldots) \\
- 2(m' - 1)(m' - 2)(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA', B', C' \hspace{-2pt} f\mathfrak{d}A', \mathfrak{d}B', \mathfrak{d}C'),
\end{multline*}
\begin{multline*}
2(m - 1)\mathfrak{d}U(\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa, \ldots) = 2(m' - 1)\mathfrak{d}U'(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa', \ldots) \\
- 2(m - 1)(\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C \hspace{-2pt} f\mathfrak{d}A, \mathfrak{d}B, \mathfrak{d}C) \\
- 2(m' - 1)(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA', B', C' \hspace{-2pt} f\mathfrak{d}A', \mathfrak{d}B', \mathfrak{d}C'),
\end{multline*}
equations which may be verified by remarking that their sum is
\begin{multline*}
m(m - 1)\{\mathfrak{d}U(\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa, \ldots) + U[(\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\mathfrak{d}a, \ldots) + (\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa, \ldots)]\} \\
- (m - 1)^2\{(\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C)^2 + (\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C \hspace{-2pt} f\mathfrak{d}A, \mathfrak{d}B, \mathfrak{d}C)\} = m'(m' - 1)\, \&\text{c.},
\end{multline*}
viz., this is the derivative with $\mathfrak{d}$ of the equation
\[
m(m - 1)U \cdot (\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa, \ldots) - (m - 1)^2(A', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C)^2 = m'(m' - 1)\, \&\text{c.}
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Taking now $U' = H$, and therefore $m' = 3m - 6$; putting also $U = 0$, $\mathfrak{d}U = 0$, and writing as before
\begin{align*}
E_\Phi &= (\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA', B', C)^2, \\
F_\Phi &= (\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA', B', C \hspace{-2pt} f\mathfrak{d}A', \mathfrak{d}B', \mathfrak{d}C'), \\
E_\Psi &= (\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C)^2, \\
F_\Psi &= (\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C \hspace{-2pt} f\mathfrak{d}A, \mathfrak{d}B, \mathfrak{d}C), \\
\Omega_g &= (\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa', \ldots), \\
\Omega_p &= (\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\mathfrak{d}a', \ldots),
\end{align*}
then the three equations are
\begin{align*}
-2(m - 1)(m - 2)F_\Phi &= (3m - 6)(3m - 7)H\Omega_g - (3m - 7)^2E_\Phi, \\
-(m - 1)^2E_\Psi &= (3m - 7)(3m - 8)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H + (3m - 6)(3m - 7)H\Omega_p - 2(3m - 7)(3m - 8)F_\Psi, \\
-2(m - 1)F_\Psi &= 2(3m - 7)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H - 2(2m - 7)F_\Psi,
\end{align*}
whence, adding, we have
\begin{multline*}
-(m - 1)^2(E_\Phi + 2F_\Phi) = -(3m - 7)^2(E_\Phi + 2F_\Phi) \\
+ (3m - 6)(3m - 7)\{\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H + H(\Omega_g + F_\Phi)\},
\end{multline*}
(that is
\[
-(m - 1)^2\mathfrak{d}_x^\Omega = -(3m - 7)^2\mathfrak{d}_x^\Omega + (3m - 6)(3m - 7)\mathfrak{d}.\Omega H,
\]
which is right).

And by linearly combining the three equations, we deduce
\begin{align*}
(3m - 6)(3m - 7)H\Omega_g &= -2(m - 1)(m - 2)F_\Phi + (3m - 7)^2E_\Phi, \\
(3m - 7)\Omega\mathfrak{d}_1 H &= -(m - 1)E_\Psi + (3m - 7)F_\Psi, \\
(3m - 6)(3m - 7)H\Omega_p &= (m - 1)(3m - 8)F_\Psi + (3m - 7)(3m - 8)F_\Psi - (m - 1)^2E_\Psi,
\end{align*}
which are the formul\ae, ante, No.~24.
\end{art}

\subsection*{Article Nos.\ 47 to 50.---Proof of an identity used in the fourth transformation, viz. $\Jac(U, \nabla H, H) = -\frac{3(m - 7)}{m - 1}F_\Phi$.}

\begin{art}
We have
\begin{align*}
\nabla &= (\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z) \\
&= ((\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{F}, \mathfrak{G} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu), \; (\mathfrak{F}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{H} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu), \; (\mathfrak{G}, \mathfrak{H}, \mathfrak{C} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu) \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z);
\end{align*}
or, attending to the effect of the bar as denoting the exemption of the $(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots)$ from differentiation,
\begin{multline*}
\Jac(U, H, \nabla H) = (\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{F}, \mathfrak{G} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu)\Jac(U, H, \partial_x H) \\
+ (\mathfrak{F}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{H} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu)\Jac(U, H, \partial_y H) \\
+ (\mathfrak{G}, \mathfrak{H}, \mathfrak{C} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu)\Jac(U, H, \partial_z H).
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Now
\[
\Jac(U, H, \partial_x H) = -\frac{3}{3m - 7}\Jac(U, x\partial_x H + y\partial_y H + z\partial_z H, \partial_x H),
\]
and the last-mentioned Jacobian is
\begin{multline*}
= \partial_x H\Jac(U, x, \partial_x H) + \partial_y H\Jac(U, y, \partial_x H) + \partial_z H\Jac(U, z, \partial_x H) \\
+ y\Jac(U, \partial_y H, \partial_x H) + z\Jac(U, \partial_z H, \partial_x H),
\end{multline*}
where the second line is
\[
= -y\Jac(U, \partial_x H, \partial_y H) + z\Jac(U, \partial_z H, \partial_x H),
\]
or writing $(A', B', C')$ for the first differential coefficients and $(a', h', c', f', g', h')$ for the second differential coefficients of $H$, this is
\[
= -y(\mathfrak{G}', \mathfrak{H}', \mathfrak{C}' \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C) + z(\mathfrak{F}', \mathfrak{B}', \mathfrak{H}' \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C).
\]

The first line is
\[
\begin{vmatrix} A & B & C \\ A' & B' & C' \\ a' & h' & g' \end{vmatrix}
= A(B'g' - C'h') + B(C'a' - A'g') + C(A'h' - B'a'),
\]
or reducing by the formul\ae,
\[
(3m - 7)(A', B', C') = (a'x + h'y + g'z, \; h'x + b'y + f'z, \; g'x + f'y + c'z),
\]
\begin{align*}
&= \frac{1}{3m - 7}\{A(-\mathfrak{G}'y + \mathfrak{H}'z) + B(-\mathfrak{F}'y + \mathfrak{B}'z) + C(-\mathfrak{G}'x + \mathfrak{A}'z)\} \\
&= \frac{1}{3m - 7}\{-y(\mathfrak{G}', \mathfrak{H}', \mathfrak{C}' \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C) + z(\mathfrak{F}', \mathfrak{B}', \mathfrak{H}' \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C)\}.
\end{align*}

Hence we have
\begin{align*}
\Jac(U, H, \partial_x H) &= -\frac{3}{3m - 7}(1 + \frac{1}{3m - 7}) \\
&\quad \{-y(\mathfrak{G}', \mathfrak{H}', \mathfrak{C}' \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C) + z(\mathfrak{F}', \mathfrak{B}', \mathfrak{H}' \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C)\};
\end{align*}
and in like manner
\begin{align*}
\Jac(U, H, \partial_y H) &= -\frac{3}{3m - 7}(1 + \frac{1}{3m - 7}) \\
&\quad \{-z(\mathfrak{W}', \mathfrak{F}', \mathfrak{G}' \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C) + x(\mathfrak{G}', \mathfrak{H}', \mathfrak{C}' \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C)\}, \\
\Jac(U, H, \partial_z H) &= -\frac{3}{3m - 7}(1 + \frac{1}{3m - 7}) \\
&\quad \{-x(\mathfrak{F}', \mathfrak{B}', \mathfrak{H}' \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C) + y(\mathfrak{W}', \mathfrak{F}', \mathfrak{G}' \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C)\}.
\end{align*}
\end{art}

\begin{art}
We thence have
\begin{multline*}
\Jac(U, H, \nabla H) = \frac{1}{3m - 7}(1 + \frac{1}{3m - 7}) \\
\begin{vmatrix}
(\mathfrak{A}', \mathfrak{F}', \mathfrak{G}' \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C) & (\mathfrak{F}', \mathfrak{B}', \mathfrak{H}' \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C) & (\mathfrak{G}', \mathfrak{H}', \mathfrak{C}' \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C) \\
x & y & z \\
\lambda & \mu & \nu
\end{vmatrix}
\end{multline*}
or multiplying the two sides by
\[
H = \begin{vmatrix} a & h & g \\ h & b & f \\ g & f & c \end{vmatrix},
\]
the right-hand side is
\begin{align*}
&= \frac{1}{3m - 7}(1 + \frac{1}{3m - 7}) \begin{vmatrix} H\lambda & H\mu & H\nu \\ x & y & z \\ (m - 1)A & (m - 1)B & (m - 1)C \end{vmatrix} \\
&= H \cdot \frac{m - 1}{3m - 7}(1 + \frac{1}{3m - 7}) \begin{vmatrix} \lambda & \mu & \nu \\ x & y & z \\ A & B & C \end{vmatrix}
\end{align*}
if for a moment
\begin{align*}
X &= (\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C \hspace{-2pt} fa, h, g), \\
Y &= (\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C \hspace{-2pt} fh, b, f), \\
Z &= (\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C \hspace{-2pt} fg, f, c).
\end{align*}
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Hence observing that these equations may be written
\begin{align*}
X &= (\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x A, \partial_x B, \partial_x C), \\
Y &= (\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_y A, \partial_y B, \partial_y C), \\
Z &= (\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_z A, \partial_z B, \partial_z C),
\end{align*}
and that we have
\[
\begin{vmatrix} \lambda & \mu & \nu \\ \partial_x & \partial_y & \partial_z \\ A & B & C \end{vmatrix} = \mathfrak{d},
\]
we obtain for $H\Jac(U, H, \nabla H)$ the value
\[
= H \cdot \frac{m - 1}{3m - 7}(1 + \frac{1}{3m - 7})(\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA, B, C \hspace{-2pt} f\mathfrak{d}A, \mathfrak{d}B, \mathfrak{d}C),
\]
or throwing out the factor $H$, we have the required result.
\end{art}

\subsection*{Article Nos.\ 51 to 53.---Proof of identity used in the fourth transformation, viz.\ $\Jac(U, \nabla, H)H = E_\Psi$, or say $\Jac(U, H, \nabla)H = (\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA', B', C')$.}

\begin{art}
We have
\[
(\mathfrak{d}_x.\nabla)H = (\partial_x\mathfrak{A}, \partial_x\mathfrak{F}, \partial_x\mathfrak{G} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu), \; (\partial_x\mathfrak{F}, \partial_x\mathfrak{B}, \partial_x\mathfrak{H} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu), \; (\partial_x\mathfrak{G}, \partial_x\mathfrak{H}, \partial_x\mathfrak{C} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu) \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x H, \partial_y H, \partial_z H),
\]
and thence
\begin{multline*}
(\mathfrak{d}_x.\nabla)H = (\partial_x\mathfrak{A}, \partial_x\mathfrak{F}, \partial_x\mathfrak{G} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu), \; (\partial_x\mathfrak{F}, \partial_x\mathfrak{B}, \partial_x\mathfrak{H} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu), \\
(\partial_x\mathfrak{G}, \partial_x\mathfrak{H}, \partial_x\mathfrak{C} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu) \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x H, \partial_y H, \partial_z H) \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu),
\end{multline*}
with the like values for $(\mathfrak{d}_y.\nabla)H$ and $(\mathfrak{d}_z.\nabla)H$. And then
\[
\Jac(U, H, \nabla)H = \begin{vmatrix} A & B & C \\ A' & B' & C' \\ (\mathfrak{d}_x.\nabla)H & (\mathfrak{d}_y.\nabla)H & (\mathfrak{d}_z.\nabla)H \end{vmatrix}
\]
in which the coefficient of $A'^2$ is
\[
= (C\partial_y - B\partial_z)(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{F}, \mathfrak{G} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu);
\]
or putting for shortness
\[
(C\partial_y - B\partial_z, \; A\partial_z - C\partial_x, \; B\partial_x - A\partial_y) = (P, Q, R);
\]
the coefficient is
\[
(P\mathfrak{A}, P\mathfrak{F}, P\mathfrak{G} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu).
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
We have
\[
\mathfrak{d} = (P\lambda + Q\mu + R\nu),
\]
and thence
\begin{align*}
\text{coefficient } A'^2 - \mathfrak{d}_x^\mathfrak{A} &= (P\mathfrak{A}, P\mathfrak{F}, P\mathfrak{G} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu) - (P\mathfrak{A}, Q\mathfrak{A}, R\mathfrak{A} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu) \\
&= \mu\{(C\partial_y - B\partial_z)\mathfrak{F} - (A\partial_z - C\partial_x)\mathfrak{A}\} \\
&\quad + \nu\{(C\partial_y - B\partial_z)\mathfrak{G} - (A\partial_y - B\partial_x)\mathfrak{A}\},
\end{align*}
where coefficient of $\mu$ is
\begin{align*}
&= -A\partial_y\mathfrak{A} - B\partial_y\mathfrak{F} + C(\partial_y\mathfrak{G} + \partial_x\mathfrak{A}) \\
&= -(A\partial_y\mathfrak{A} + B\partial_y\mathfrak{F} + C\partial_y\mathfrak{G}) = -\frac{x\partial_y H}{m - 1},
\end{align*}
and coefficient of $\nu$ is
\[
= +(A\partial_z\mathfrak{A} + B\partial_z\mathfrak{F} + C\partial_z\mathfrak{G}) = \frac{x\partial_z H}{m - 1},
\]
so that
\[
\text{coefficient } A'^2 - \mathfrak{d}_x^\mathfrak{A} = -\frac{x}{m - 1}(\mu\partial_y H - \nu\partial_z H).
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
By forming in a similar manner the coefficients of the other terms, it appears that
\[
\Jac(U, H, \nabla)H - (\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA', B', C') = 0,
\]
or since the determinant is
\[
\begin{vmatrix} A' & B' & C' \\ A' & B' & C' \\ (\mathfrak{d}_x.\nabla)H & (\mathfrak{d}_y.\nabla)H & (\mathfrak{d}_z.\nabla)H \end{vmatrix} = 0,
\]
or
\[
\begin{vmatrix} \lambda & \mu & \nu \\ \partial_x H & \partial_y H & \partial_z H \\ A' & B' & C' \end{vmatrix} = \ldots
\]
we have the required equation,
\[
\Jac(U, H, \nabla)H = (\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{A}', \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fA', B', C').
\]
This completes the series of formul\ae\ used in the transformations of the condition for the sextactic point.
\end{art}

\subsection*{Appendix, Nos.\ 54 to 74.}

For the sake of exhibiting in their proper connexion some of the formul\ae\ employed in the foregoing first transformation of the condition for a sextactic point, I have investigated them in the present Appendix, which however is numbered continuously with the memoir.

\begin{art}
The investigations of my former memoir and the present memoir have reference to the operations
\begin{align*}
\mathfrak{d}_1 &= dx\,\partial_x + dy\,\partial_y + dz\,\partial_z, \\
\mathfrak{d}_2 &= d^2x\,\partial_x + d^2y\,\partial_y + d^2z\,\partial_z, \\
&\quad \&\text{c.}, \\
\mathfrak{d}_5 &= d^5x\,\partial_x + d^5y\,\partial_y + d^5z\,\partial_z,
\end{align*}
where if $(A, B, C)$ are the first differential coefficients of a function $U = (* \hspace{-2pt} fx, y, z)^m$, and $\lambda$, $\mu$, $\nu$ are arbitrary constants, then we have
\[
dx = B\nu - C\mu, \quad dy = C\lambda - A\nu, \quad dz = A\mu - B\lambda;
\]
so that putting
\[
\mathfrak{d} = (B\nu - C\mu)\partial_x + (C\lambda - A\nu)\partial_y + (A\mu - B\lambda)\partial_z = \begin{vmatrix} A & B & C \\ \lambda & \mu & \nu \\ \partial_x & \partial_y & \partial_z \end{vmatrix},
\]
we have $\mathfrak{d}_1 = \mathfrak{d}$. The foregoing expressions of $(dx, dy, dz)$ determine of course the values of $(d^2x, d^2y, d^2z)$, $(d^3x, d^3y, d^3z)$, \&c., and it is throughout assumed that these values are substituted in the symbols $\mathfrak{d}_2$, $\mathfrak{d}_3$, \&c., so that $\mathfrak{d}_1 = \mathfrak{d}$, and $\mathfrak{d}_2$, $\mathfrak{d}_3$, \&c.\ denote each of them an operator such as $X\partial_x + Y\partial_y + Z\partial_z$, where $(X, Y, Z)$ are functions of the coordinates; such operator, in so far as it is a function of the coordinates, may therefore be made an operand, and be operated upon by itself or any other like operator.
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Taking $(a, b, c, f, g, h)$ for the second differential coefficients of $U$, $(\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{C}, \mathfrak{F}, \mathfrak{G}, \mathfrak{H})$ for the inverse coefficients, and $H$ for the Hessian, I write also
\[
\Phi = (\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{C}, \mathfrak{F}, \mathfrak{G}, \mathfrak{H} \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu)^2,
\]
\[
\Psi = (\mathfrak{A}, \mathfrak{B}, \mathfrak{C}, \mathfrak{F}, \mathfrak{G}, \mathfrak{H} \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2 \Phi,
\]
\[
\xi = \lambda x + \mu y + \nu z,
\]
\[
\nabla = (\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x H, \partial_y H, \partial_z H)^2,
\]
\[
\Upsilon = (a, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\mu z - \nu y, \nu x - \lambda z, \lambda y - \mu x)^2,
\]
and I notice that we have
\[
\Upsilon = 2\Phi, \quad \nabla\Upsilon = 2\Psi H, \quad \mathfrak{d}\Upsilon = 3H,
\]
the last of which is proved, post No.~65; the others are found without any difficulty.
\end{art}

\begin{art}
I form the Table
\begin{align*}
\mathfrak{d}_1 U &= \frac{m - 1}{(m - 1)}\Phi, \\
\mathfrak{d}_1^2 U &= \frac{1}{(m - 1)^2}\{-3(m - 2)H\Phi + (m - 1)\Phi\mathfrak{d}_1 H\}, \\
\mathfrak{d}_1^3 U &= \frac{1}{(m - 1)^3}\{(18m^2 - 66m + 60)H^2\Phi + \ldots\}, \\
\mathfrak{d}_1^4 U &= \frac{1}{(m - 1)^4}\{(-162m^3 + \ldots)H^3\Phi + \ldots\}, \\
\mathfrak{d}_1^5 U &= \ldots
\end{align*}
and assuming $U = 0$,
\begin{align*}
(\mathfrak{d}_1 H)^2 &= (\mathfrak{d}H)^2 = -\frac{\Psi^2}{(m - 1)^2}H + \ldots, \\
\mathfrak{d}_1^2 H &= \frac{1}{(m - 1)^2}\{(-6m^2 + 18m - 12)H\Phi^2 + \ldots\}, \\
&\quad \&\text{c.},
\end{align*}
which are for the most part given in my former memoir; the expressions for $\mathfrak{d}_2 U$, $\mathfrak{d}_3 U$, which are not explicitly given, follow at once from the equations
\[
(\mathfrak{d}_1^2 + \mathfrak{d}_2)U = 0, \quad (\mathfrak{d}_1^3 + 2\mathfrak{d}_1\mathfrak{d}_2 + \mathfrak{d}_3)U = 0;
\]
those for $\mathfrak{d}_1\mathfrak{d}_3 U$, $\mathfrak{d}_2^2 U$, and $\mathfrak{d}_5 U$ are new, but when the expressions for $\mathfrak{d}_1\mathfrak{d}_3 U$ and $\mathfrak{d}_4 U$ are known, that for $\mathfrak{d}_5 U$ is at once found from the equation
\[
(\mathfrak{d}_1^5 + 6\mathfrak{d}_1^2\mathfrak{d}_3 + 4\mathfrak{d}_1\mathfrak{d}_3 + 3\mathfrak{d}_2^2 + \mathfrak{d}_5)U = 0.
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Before going further, I remark that we have identically
\begin{multline*}
(a, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fx, y, z)^2(a, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\mu z - \nu y, \nu x - \lambda z, \lambda y - \mu x)^2 \\
= (\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu \hspace{-2pt} f\mu z - \nu y, \nu x - \lambda z, \lambda y - \mu x)^2
\end{multline*}
(if for shortness $p = ax + hy + gz$, $q = \lambda x + \mu y + \nu z$)
\[
= p^2(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu)^2 - 2pq(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\lambda, \mu, \nu \hspace{-2pt} fa, b, c, 2f, 2g, 2h) + q^2(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} fa, b, c, 2f, 2g, 2h)^2.
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
If in this equation we take $(a, b, c, f, g, h)$ to be the second differential coefficients of $U$, and write also $(a, b, c) = (\partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)$, the equation becomes
\begin{multline*}
m(m - 1)U\Upsilon - (m - 1)^2\Phi^2 = \xi^2(x\partial_x + y\partial_y + z\partial_z)^2 \\
- 2\xi(x\partial_x + y\partial_y + z\partial_z)\nabla + \nabla^2(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2,
\end{multline*}
which is a general equation for the transformation of $\mathfrak{d}_2^2$ ($= \mathfrak{d}_x^2$).
\end{art}

\begin{art}
If with the two sides of this equation we operate on $U$, we obtain
\[
m(m - 1)\Upsilon U - (m - 1)^2\mathfrak{d}_2^2 U = m(m - 1)\Phi^2 U - 2(m - 1)\Phi\nabla\Phi + \nabla^2(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2 U,
\]
and substituting the values
\[
\Upsilon = 2\Phi, \quad \mathfrak{d}_1^2 U = \ldots,
\]
we find the before-mentioned expression of $\mathfrak{d}_2^2 U$.
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Operating with the two sides of the same equation on a function $H$ of the order $m'$, we find
\[
m(m - 1)\Upsilon H - (m - 1)^2\mathfrak{d}_2^2 H = m'(m' - 1)\Phi^2 H - 2(m' - 1)\Phi\nabla\Phi + \nabla^2(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2 H;
\]
and in particular if $H$ is the Hessian, then writing $m' = 3m - 6$, and putting $U = 0$, we find the before-mentioned expression for $\mathfrak{d}_2^2 H$.
\end{art}

\begin{art}
But we may also from the general identical equation deduce the expression for $(\mathfrak{d}H)^2$. In fact taking $H$ a function of the degree $m'$ and writing
\[
(a, \beta, \gamma) = (\partial_x H, \partial_y H, \partial_z H),
\]
we have
\begin{multline*}
m(m - 1)U(a, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\mu\partial_z H - \nu\partial_y H, \nu\partial_x H - \lambda\partial_z H, \lambda\partial_y H - \mu\partial_x H)^2 - (m - 1)^2(\mathfrak{d}H)^2 \\
= m'(m' - 1)\Phi^2 H - 2m'\Phi\nabla H + \nabla^2(\mathfrak{A}, \ldots \hspace{-2pt} f\partial_x H, \partial_y H, \partial_z H)^2;
\end{multline*}
and if $H$ be the Hessian, then writing $m' = 3m - 6$ and putting also $U = 0$, we find the before-mentioned expression for $(\mathfrak{d}H)^2$.
\end{art}

\begin{art}
\textit{Proof of equation}
\[
\frac{1}{m - 1}(\lambda\partial_x + \mu\partial_y + \nu\partial_z) + \ldots = \frac{\Psi}{m - 1}.
\]
We have
\[
\ldots = (\lambda(C\partial_y - B\partial_z) + \mu(A\partial_z - C\partial_x) + \nu(B\partial_x - A\partial_y)),
\]
which is
\[
\lambda(C'\partial_y - B'\partial_z) + \mu(A'\partial_z - C'\partial_x) + \nu(B'\partial_x - A'\partial_y),
\]
where
\begin{align*}
A' &= \mathfrak{d}A = a(B\nu - C\mu) + h(C\lambda - A\nu) + g(A\mu - B\lambda) \\
&= \lambda(hC - gB) + \mu(gA - aC) + \nu(aB - hA),
\end{align*}
with the like values for $B'$ and $C'$. Substituting the values
\[
(m - 1)(A, B, C) = (ax + hy + gz, \; hx + by + fz, \; gx + fy + cz),
\]
we have
\[
(m - 1)A' = \lambda(\mathfrak{G}y - \mathfrak{H}z) + \mu(\mathfrak{H}x - \mathfrak{G}z) + \nu(\mathfrak{G}x - \mathfrak{F}z);
\]
and similarly
\begin{align*}
(m - 1)B' &= \lambda(\mathfrak{H}z - \mathfrak{G}x) + \mu(\mathfrak{F}z - \mathfrak{H}x) + \nu(\mathfrak{H}x - \mathfrak{G}y), \\
(m - 1)C' &= \lambda(\mathfrak{F}x - \mathfrak{B}y) + \mu(\mathfrak{A}y - \mathfrak{F}x) + \nu(\mathfrak{B}x - \mathfrak{A}y).
\end{align*}
\end{art}
\clearpage

%====================================================================
\section{341. On the Sextactic Points of a Plane Curve.}

[From the \textit{Philosophical Transactions}, vol.\ CLIV. (for the year 1864),
pp.~545--578. Received \textit{October 15},---Read \textit{December 10}, 1863.]

[Continued from previous pages.]

\setcounter{art}{9}
\begin{art}
And by means of these the condition becomes
\begin{multline*}
0 = \frac{1}{(m-1)^4} \nu^2 \bigl\{(153m^2 - 594m + 549) H^2 d\Phi \\
+ (-102m^2 + 396m + 366) \Phi dH\bigr\} \\
+ \frac{1}{(m-1)^3} \nu \bigl\{(-96m + 168) H(\partial . \nabla)H
+ (-90m + 162) H d'^2 H + (120m - 240) dH \nabla H\bigr\} \\
+ \frac{1}{(m-1)^2} \bigl\{9H^2 \partial \Omega - 45 H \Omega \partial H
+ 40 \Omega^2 \partial H\bigr\},
\end{multline*}
being, as already remarked, of the degree 5 in the arbitrary coefficients
$(\lambda, \mu, \nu)$, and of the order $12m - 22$ in the coordinates $(x, y, z)$.
\end{art}

\begin{art}
But throwing out the factor $\nu^2$ and observing that in the first line the
quadric functions of $m$ are each a numerical multiple of $51m^2 - 198m + 183$, the
condition becomes
\begin{multline*}
0 = (51m^2 - 198m + 183) H^2 (3H d\Phi - 2\Phi dH) \\
+ \nu \bigl\{(-96m + 168) H^2 (\partial . \nabla)H + (-90m + 162) H^2 \partial \nabla H
+ (120m - 240) H dH \nabla H\bigr\} \\
+ \nu^2 \bigl\{9H^2 \partial \Omega - 45H\Omega \partial H + 40 \Omega^2 \partial H\bigr\}.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\subsection*{Article Nos.\ 12 and 13.---Second transformation.}

\setcounter{art}{11}
\begin{art}
We effect this by means of the formula
\[
(m-2)(3H \partial \Phi - 2\Phi \partial H) = -\frac{3}{m-2} \Jac(U, \Phi, H),
\tag{J}
\]
for substituting this value of $(3H \partial \Phi - 2\Phi \partial H)$ the equation becomes
divisible by $\nu$; and dividing out accordingly, the condition becomes
\begin{multline*}
\frac{51m^2 - 198m + 183}{m-2} \nu^2 H^2 \Jac(U, \Phi, H) \\
+ (-96m + 168) \nu H^2 (\partial . \nabla)H + (-90m + 162) H^2 \partial \nabla H
+ (120m - 240) H dH \nabla H \\
+ \nu^2 \bigl\{9H^2 \partial \Omega - 45H\Omega \partial H + 40\Omega^2 \partial H\bigr\} = 0.
\end{multline*}
(J) here and elsewhere refers to the Jacobian Formula, see post, Article Nos.\ 34 and 35.
\end{art}

\begin{art}
We have (see post, Article Nos.\ 36 to 40)
\[
\Jac(U, \Phi, H) = -(\partial . \nabla)H;
\]
and introducing also $d.\nabla H$ in place of $\partial \nabla H$ by means of the formula
\[
-(6m-6)H^2 (\partial . \nabla)H
\]
the condition becomes
\begin{multline*}
\frac{51m^2 - 198m + 183}{m-2} H^2 (-(\partial . \nabla)H) \\
+ (-90m + 162) H^2 \partial (\nabla H) + 120(m-2) H dH \nabla H \\
+ \nu^2 \bigl\{9H^2 \partial \Omega - 45H\Omega \partial H + 40\Omega^2 \partial H\bigr\} = 0,
\end{multline*}
or, as this may be written,
\begin{multline*}
(45m^2 - 180m + 171) H^2 (\partial . \nabla)H \\
+ (-90m + 162)(m-2) H^2 \partial (\nabla H) + 120(m-2)^2 H dH \nabla H \\
+ (m-2) \nu^2 \bigl\{9H^2 \partial \Omega - 45H\Omega \partial H + 40\Omega^2 \partial H\bigr\} = 0.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\subsection*{Article Nos.\ 14 to 17.---Third transformation.}

\setcounter{art}{13}
\begin{art}
We have the following formul\ae,
\begin{align}
&\Jac(U, \nabla H, H) - (5m-11)\partial H \nabla H + (3m-6)H \partial(\nabla H) = 0,
\tag{J} \\
&\Jac(U, \nabla, H)H - (5m-11)\partial H \nabla H + (3m-6)H (\partial . \nabla)H = 0,
\tag{J}
\end{align}
in the latter of which, treating $\nabla$ as a function of the coordinates, we first form the
symbol $\Jac(U, \nabla, H)$, and then operating therewith on $H$, we have
$\Jac(U, \nabla, H)H$; these give
\[
H(\partial . \nabla)H = \frac{1}{5m-11}\bigl\{(3m-6)H \partial(\nabla H) - \Jac(U, \nabla, H)H\bigr\},
\]
\[
H(\partial . \nabla)H = \frac{1}{5m-11}\bigl\{(3m-6)H(\partial . \nabla)H - \Jac(U, \nabla, H)H\bigr\};
\]
and substituting these values, the resulting coefficient of $H dH \nabla H$ is
\[
(45m^2 - 180m + 171)\frac{1}{5m-11} + (-90m + 162)\frac{3m-6}{5m-11} + 120(m-2)^2,
\]
which is $=0$.
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Hence the condition will contain the factor $\nu$, and throwing out this, and
also the constant factor $\frac{1}{m-2}$, it becomes
\begin{multline*}
(-15m^2 + 60m - 57) H \Jac(U, \nabla, H)H \\
+ (30m - 54)(m-2) H \Jac(U, \nabla H, H) \\
+ (m-2)^2 \bigl\{9H^2 \partial \Omega - 45H\Omega \partial H + 40\Omega^2 \partial H\bigr\} = 0.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\begin{art}
We have
\begin{align*}
\Jac(U, \nabla H, H) &= \Jac(U, \nabla, H)H + \Jac(U, H\nabla, H), \\
\intertext{viz. in $(\partial_x \cdot \nabla)H$, treating $\nabla$ as a function of $(x, y, z)$
we operate upon it with $\partial_x$ to obtain the new symbol $\partial_x \nabla$, and with this
we operate on $H$; in $\partial_x \nabla$ we simply multiply together the symbols
$\partial_x$ and $\nabla$, giving a new symbol of the form $(\partial_x^2, \partial_x\partial_y, \partial_x\partial_z)$
which then operates on $H$. We have the like values of
$\partial_y(\nabla H)$ and $\partial_z(\nabla H)$; and thence also}
\Jac(U, \nabla H, H) &= \Jac(U, \nabla, H)H + \Jac(U, H\nabla, H),
\end{align*}
viz. in the determinant $\Jac(U, \nabla, H)$ the second line corresponding to $\nabla$ is
$\partial_x \nabla$, $\partial_y \nabla$, $\partial_z \nabla$ ($\nabla$ being the operand); and the Jacobian thus
obtained is a symbol which operates on $H$ giving $\Jac(U, \nabla, H)H$; and in the
determinant $\Jac(U, \nabla H, H)$ the second line is $\partial_x H$, $\partial_y \nabla H$, $\partial_z \nabla H$
($\nabla$ being simply multiplied by $\partial_x$, $\partial_y$, $\partial_z$ respectively).
\end{art}

\setcounter{art}{16}
\begin{art}
Substituting, the condition becomes
\begin{multline*}
(-15m^2 + 60m - 57) H \Jac(U, \nabla, H)H \\
+ (30m - 54)(m-2)\bigl\{H^2 \Jac(U, \nabla, H)H + \Jac(U, H\nabla, H)\bigr\} \\
+ (m-2)^2 \bigl\{9H^2 \partial \Omega - 45H\Omega \partial H + 40\Omega^2 \partial H\bigr\} = 0,
\end{multline*}
or, what is the same thing,
\begin{multline*}
(15m^2 - 54m + 51) H^2 \Jac(U, \nabla, H)H \\
+ (30m - 54)(m-2)H \Jac(U, H\nabla, H) \\
+ (m-2)^2 \bigl\{9H^2 \partial \Omega - 45H\Omega \partial H + 40\Omega^2 \partial H\bigr\} = 0.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\subsection*{Article Nos.\ 18 to 27.---Fourth transformation, and final form of the
condition for a Sextactic Point.}

\setcounter{art}{17}
\begin{art}
I write
\begin{align}
&(5m - 12)\Omega \partial H - (3m - 6)H \partial \Omega = \frac{3}{m-2} \Jac(U, \Omega, H),
\tag{J} \\
&\Omega \partial H + H \partial \Omega = \partial(\Omega H). \notag
\end{align}
and, introducing for convenience the new symbol $\fW$,
\[
-5\fW H + H \partial \Omega = \fW,
\]
so that
\[
\begin{vmatrix}
5m-12, & -(3m-6), & \frac{3}{m-2}\Jac(U, \Omega, H) \\
1, & 1, & \partial(\Omega H) \\
-5, & 1, & \fW
\end{vmatrix}
= 0,
\]
or, what is the same thing,
\[
(8m - 18)\fW + 6\partial \Jac(U, \Omega, H) + (10m - 18)\partial(\Omega H) = 0,
\]
we have
\[
\fW = \partial \Omega H - 5\Omega \partial H
= \frac{-3}{4m-9}\Jac(U, \Omega, H) - \frac{6(m-2)}{4m-9}\partial(\Omega H).
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
We have also
\[
(8m-18)H \partial \Omega - (3m-6)\Omega \partial H - \frac{3}{m-2}\Jac(U, \Omega, H) = 0,
\tag{J}
\]
that is
\[
H \partial \Omega = \frac{3m-6}{8m-18}\Omega \partial H
+ \frac{3}{(m-2)(8m-18)}\Jac(U, \Omega, H),
\]
and thence
\begin{multline*}
\partial H \cdot \fW + \fW \partial H
= 9H^2 \partial \Omega - 45H\Omega \partial H + 40\Omega^2 \partial H, \\
- \frac{9(5m-9)}{(4m-9)^2} H \Jac(U, \Omega, H)
- \frac{60(m-2)}{(4m-9)^2} \Omega \Jac(U, \Omega, H) \\
+ \frac{1}{(4m-9)^2}\{-27H \Jac(U, \Omega, H) + 40\Jac(U, \Omega, H)\}.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\setcounter{art}{19}
\begin{art}
The condition thus becomes
\begin{multline*}
(15m^2 - 54m + 51)(4m - 9)H^2 \Jac(U, \nabla, H)H \\
+ 6(5m - 9)(m-2)(4m-9)H \Jac(U, H\nabla, H) \\
+ 3(m-2)\bigl\{-3(5m-9)(m-2)H \partial(\Omega H) + 20(m-2)^2 \nabla \Omega\bigr\} \\
+ (m-2)^2 \nu^2\{-27H\Jac(U, \Omega, H) + 40\Jac(U, \Omega, H)\} = 0,
\end{multline*}
which for shortness I represent by
\[
3H\fN + (m-2)^2 \nu^2\{-27H\Jac(U, \Omega, H) + 40\Jac(U, \Omega, H)\} = 0,
\]
so that we have
\begin{multline*}
\fN = (5m^2 - 18m + 17)(4m-9)\Jac(U, \nabla, H)H \\
+ 2(5m-9)(m-2)(4m-9)\Jac(U, H\nabla, H) \\
+ (m-2)\{-3(5m-9)(m-2)\partial(\Omega H) + 20(m-2)^2 \nabla \Omega\}.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Write
\[
\Phi' = (\fApr, \fBpr, \fCpr, \fFpr, \fGpr, \fHpr \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} A, B, C),
\]
where $(A, B, C)$ are as before the differential coefficients of $U$, and
$(a', b', c', f', g', h')$ being the second differential coefficients of $H$,
$(\fApr, \fBpr, \fCpr, \fFpr, \fGpr, \fHpr)$ are the inverse coefficients, viz.
$\fApr = b'c' - f'^2$, \&c.\ We have
\[
-(m-1)^2 \partial^2 \Phi' = (3m-6)(3m-7)\partial(\Omega H) - (3m-7)^2 \partial^2 \Omega
\]
(see post, Nos.\ 41 to 46),
that is
\[
(3m-6)\partial(\Omega H) = (3m-7)\partial^2 \Omega - \frac{(m-1)^2}{(3m-7)}\partial^2 \Phi'.
\]
\end{art}

\setcounter{art}{21}
\begin{art}
Now
\[
\Phi = (\fA, \fB, \fC, \fF, \fG, \fH \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} A, B, C), \quad
\Phi' = (\fApr, \fBpr, \fCpr, \fGpr, \fHpr \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} A, B, C),
\]
and writing for shortness
\begin{align*}
E_\Phi &= (\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} A', B', C), &
F_\Phi &= (\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial A', \partial B', \partial C'), \\
E_{\Phi'} &= (\fApr, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} A, B, C)^2, &
F_{\Phi'} &= (\fApr, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} A, B, C \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial A, \partial B, \partial C),
\end{align*}
(we might, in a notation above explained, write $E_\Phi = \partial \fN \Phi$,
$F_\Phi = \fM \Phi$, and in like manner $E_{\Phi'} = \partial \fN \Phi'$,
$F_{\Phi'} = \fM \Phi'$), then we have
\[
\partial^2 \Phi = E_\Phi + 2F_\Phi, \quad
\partial^2 \Phi' = E_{\Phi'} + 2F_{\Phi'}.
\]
We have moreover
\[
\Jac(U, \nabla H, H) = -\frac{3m-7}{(m-1)^2} F_\Phi, \quad
\text{post, Nos.\ 47 to 50},
\]
\[
\Jac(U, \nabla, H)H = -E_\Phi, \quad
\text{post, Nos.\ 51 to 53}.
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
The just-mentioned formul\ae\ give
\begin{multline*}
\fN = -(5m^2 - 18m + 17)(4m-9)E_\Phi \\
- 2(5m - 9)(m - 2)(4m - 9)\frac{(m-1)^2}{3m-7} F_\Phi \\
+ (m-2)(5m^2 - 18m + 17)(E_\Phi + 2F_\Phi) \\
- \frac{(5m-9)(m-1)^2(m-2)}{3m-7}(E_{\Phi'} + 2F_{\Phi'}),
\end{multline*}
that is
\begin{multline*}
\fN = -(3m-7)(5m^2 - 18m + 17)E_\Phi \\
+ 2(m-2)(5m^2 - 18m + 17)F_\Phi \\
+ \frac{(5m-9)(m-1)^2(m-2)}{3m-7} E_{\Phi'} \\
- \frac{2(m-1)(m-2)(3m-8)(5m-9)}{3m-7} F_{\Phi'}.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\begin{art}
But recollecting that
\[
\Phi = (\fA, \fB, \fC, \fF, \fG, \fH \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2 H
= (\fA, \fB, \fC, \fF, \fG, \fH \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a', b', c', 2f', 2g', 2h'),
\]
and putting
\begin{align*}
E_\Omega &= (a\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a', \dots) \quad (= \partial \Omega \Phi), \\
F_\Omega &= (\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a a', \dots) \quad (= \partial \Omega \Psi),
\end{align*}
we have, post, Nos.\ 41 to 46,
\begin{align*}
-2(m-1)(m-2)F_\Phi + (3m-7)^2 E_\Phi &= (3m-6)(3m-7)H E_\Omega, \\
(m-1)(3m-8)F_\Phi + (3m-7)(3m-8)F_\Phi - (m-1)^2 F_\Phi
&= (3m-6)(3m-7)H F_\Omega, \\
-(m-1)F_\Phi + (3m-7)F_\Phi &= (3m-7)\Phi F_\Omega,
\end{align*}
and the foregoing equation becomes
\begin{multline*}
(3m-7)\fN = -(5m^2 - 18m + 17)(3m-6)(3m-7)H E_\Omega \\
- (5m-9)(m-2)(3m-6)(3m-7)H F_\Omega \\
+ (m-2)(25m^2 - 103m + 106)(3m-7)\Phi \partial H.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\begin{art}
But we have
\begin{align}
&\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Phi) - (3m-6)H E_\Omega + (2m-4)\Omega \partial H = 0,
\tag{J} \\
&\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Psi) - (3m-6)H F_\Omega + (3m-8)\Omega \partial H = 0,
\tag{J}
\end{align}
that is
\begin{align*}
3(m-2)H E_\Omega &= 2(m-2)\Omega \partial H + \nu^2 \Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Phi), \\
3(m-2)H F_\Omega &= (3m-8)\Omega \partial H + \nu^2 \Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Psi),
\end{align*}
and we thus obtain
\begin{multline*}
\fN = -(5m^2 - 18m + 17)\{2(m-2)\Omega \partial H
+ \nu^2 \Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Phi)\} \\
- (5m - 9)(m-2)\{(3m-8)\Omega \partial H + \nu^2 \Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Psi)\} \\
+ (25m^2 - 103m + 106)(m-2)\Omega \partial H,
\end{multline*}
where the coefficient of $(m-2)\Omega \partial H$ is
\[
-(10m^2 - 36m + 34) - (5m-9)(3m-8) + (25m^2 - 103m + 106),
\]
which is $=0$.
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Hence
\[
\fN = -(5m^2 - 18m + 17)\nu^2 \Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Phi)
- (5m - 9)(m-2)\nu^2 \Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Psi).
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Substituting this in the equation
\[
3H\fN + (m-2)^2 \nu^2\{-27H\Jac(U, H, H) + 40\Jac(U, \Omega, H)\} = 0,
\]
the result contains the factor $\nu^2$, and, throwing this out, the condition is
\begin{multline*}
3H\{-(5m^2 - 18m + 17)\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Phi)
- (5m-9)(m-2)\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Psi)\} \\
+ (m-2)^2\{27H^2\Jac(U, H, \Omega) - 40\Jac(U, H, \Omega)\} = 0,
\end{multline*}
or, as this may also be written,
\begin{multline*}
-(15m^2 - 54m + 51)H\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Phi)
- 3(5m-9)(m-2)H\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Psi) \\
+ 27(m-2)^2\{H\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Phi) + H\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Psi)\} \\
- 40(m-2)^2 \Jac(U, \Omega, H) = 0.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Hence the condition finally is
\begin{multline*}
(12m^2 - 54m + 57)H\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Phi)
+ (m-2)(12m - 27)H\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Psi) \\
- 40(m-2)^2 \Jac(U, H, \Omega) = 0,
\end{multline*}
or, as this may also be written,
\begin{multline*}
-3(m-1)H\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Phi) + (m-2)(12m-27)H\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Psi) \\
- 40(m-2)^2 \Jac(U, H, \Omega) = 0,
\end{multline*}
viz. the sextactic points are the intersections of the curve $U=0$ with the curve
represented by this equation; and observing that $U$, $H$, $\Omega_\Phi$, and $\Omega$
are of the orders $m$, $3m-6$, $8m-18$ respectively, the order of the curve is as
above mentioned $= 12m - 27$.
\end{art}

\subsection*{Article Nos.\ 28 to 30.---Application to a Cubic.}

\setcounter{art}{27}
\begin{art}
I have in my former memoir, No.\ 30, shown that for a cubic curve
\[
\Omega = (\fA, \fB, \fC, \fF, \fG, \fH \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2 H = -2S \cdot U = 0;
\]
this implies $\Jac(U, H, \Omega) = 0$, and hence if one of the two Jacobians,
$\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Phi)$, $\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Psi)$ vanish, the other will also vanish.
Now, using the canonical form we have
\begin{align*}
\Omega &= (\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a', \dots) \\
&= (yz - l^2x^2,\; zx - l^2y^2,\; xy - l^2z^2,\; l^2yz - lx^2,\; l^2zx - ly^2,\; l^2xy - lz^2) \\
&= (-3l^2x,\; -3l^2y,\; -3l^2z,\; (1 + 2l^3)x,\; (1 + 2l^3)y,\; (1 + 2l^3)z),
\end{align*}
the development of which in fact gives the last-mentioned result. But applying this
formula to the calculation of $\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Phi)$, then disregarding numerical factors,
we have
\begin{align*}
\partial_x \Omega_\Phi &= (yz - l^2x^2, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} -3l^2, 0, 0, (1+2l^3), 0, 0) \\
&= -3l^2(yz - l^2x^2) + (1+2l^3)(l^2yz - lx^2) \\
&= (-l + l^4)(x^3 + 2lyz) = 3\partial_x U;
\end{align*}
and in like manner $\partial_y \Omega_\Phi = 3\partial_y U$, $\partial_z \Omega_\Phi = 3\partial_z U$, and therefore
\[
\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Phi) = 3\Jac(U, H, U) = 0,
\]
whence also
\[
\Jac(U, H, \Omega_\Psi) = 0;
\]
And the condition for a sextactic point assumes the more simple form,
\[
\Jac(U, H, \Psi) = 0.
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Now (former memoir, No.\ 32) we have
\begin{align*}
\Psi &= (\fA, \fB, \fC, \fF, \fG, \fH \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2 \Phi \\
&= (1 + 8l^3)^2 (x^6 + y^6 + z^6) \\
&\quad + (-9l^2)(x^3 + y^3 + z^3)^2 \\
&\quad + (-2l - 5l^4 - 20l^7)(x^3 + y^3 + z^3)xyz \\
&\quad + (-15l^3 - 78l^6 + 12l^9)x^2y^2z^2,
\end{align*}
or observing that $x^3 + y^3 + z^3$ and $xyz$, and therefore the last three lines of the
expression of $\Psi$ are functions of $U$ ($= x^3 + y^3 + z^3 + 6lxyz$) and
$H$ ($= -l^2(x^3 + y^3 + z^3) + (1 + 2l^3)xyz$), and consequently give rise to
the term $=0$ in $\Jac(U, H, \Psi)$, we may write
\[
\Psi = (1 + 8l^3)^2(x^6 + y^6 + z^6).
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
We have then, disregarding a constant factor,
\[
\Jac(U, H, \Psi) = \Jac(x^3 + y^3 + z^3,\; xyz,\; x^4y^2 + y^4z^2 + z^4x^2),
\]
or
\[
\begin{vmatrix}
x^2, & y^2, & z^2 \\
yz, & zx, & xy \\
x^2(y^4 + z^4), & y^2(z^4 + x^4), & z^2(x^4 + y^4)
\end{vmatrix}
\]
\begin{align*}
&= x^2(y^6 - z^6) + y^2(z^6 - x^6) + z^2(x^6 - y^6), \\
&= (y^2 - z^2)(z^2 - x^2)(x^2 - y^2),
\end{align*}
so that the sextactic points are the intersections of the curve
\[
U = x^3 + y^3 + z^3 + 6lxyz = 0,
\]
with the curve
\[
x^2(y^6 - z^6) + y^2(z^6 - x^6) + z^2(x^6 - y^6) = 0,
\]
or, what is the same thing,
\[
(y^2 - z^2)(z^2 - x^2)(x^2 - y^2) = 0.
\]
\end{art}

\subsection*{Article Nos.\ 31 to 33.---Proof of identities for the first transformation.}

\setcounter{art}{30}
\begin{art}
\textbf{Calculation of $(\partial_x^4 + 10\partial_x^2\partial_y\partial_z + 10\partial_x\partial_y^2\partial_z
+ 15\partial_y\partial_z^3)U$.}

Writing $\partial$ in place of $D$, we have (former memoir, No.\ 20)
\[
\partial_x^4 U = \frac{1}{(m-1)^4}\{(18m^2 - 66m + 60)\Phi \partial^2 H
+ (-10m + 18)(\partial . \nabla)H\}.
\]
But
\[
\partial^2 H = \frac{(3m-6)(3m-7)}{(m-1)^2}\Phi \partial^2 H - \frac{6m-14}{(m-1)^2}\Phi \partial H,
\]
former memoir, Nos.\ 21 and 22; and thence
\begin{multline*}
(\partial_x^4 + 6\partial_x^2\partial_y\partial_z)U \\
= \frac{1}{(m-1)^4}\{(18m^2 - 66m + 60)\Phi \partial^2 H
+ (-10m + 18)(\partial . \nabla)H\},
\end{multline*}
whence operating on each side with $\partial_x = \partial$, we have
\begin{multline*}
(\partial_x^5 + 10\partial_x^3\partial_y\partial_z + 5\partial_x^2\partial_y\partial_z^2 + 12\partial_x\partial_y\partial_z^3)U \\
= \frac{-1}{(m-1)^4}(18m^2 - 66m + 60)(\Phi \partial^3 H + \partial\Phi \partial^2 H) \\
+ \frac{1}{(m-1)^4}(-10m + 18)\{(\partial . \nabla)\partial H + \partial \nabla \partial H\}.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\setcounter{art}{31}
\begin{art}
\textbf{Calculation of $\partial_x U \partial_x H + 2\partial_y U \partial_y H + 2\partial_z U \partial_z H$.}

We have
\begin{align*}
\partial_x U &= \frac{1}{(m-1)^2}\partial_x H, &
\partial_y U &= \frac{1}{m-1}\partial_y H, &
\partial_z U &= \frac{1}{m-1}\partial_z H, \\
\partial_x H' &= \frac{1}{m-1}\{(-3m+6)\Phi \partial^2 H - \Phi \partial H
+ \frac{1}{m-1}(\partial . \nabla)H\},
\end{align*}
for which values see Appendix, No.\ 58. And hence the expression sought for is
which is
\begin{multline*}
= 2(m-1)\partial^2 \Phi \partial_x H \\
+ 2H\{(-3m+6)\Phi \partial^2 H - \Phi \partial H + \tfrac{1}{m-1}(\partial . \nabla)H\} \\
+ (m-1)\partial H \cdot \nabla H \\
+ (-6m+12)\partial^2 \Phi - 3\nu^2 \Phi \partial H \\
+ (m-1)^2\{2H(\partial . \nabla)H - \nu^2 H \nabla H\}.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

But we have, former memoir, Nos.\ 21 and 25,
\[
\partial_x \Phi = \frac{(3m-6)H \partial \Phi - \Phi \partial H}{(m-1)^2},
\quad
\partial_y \Phi = \frac{1}{m-1}\partial_y \Phi, \quad
\partial_z \Phi = \frac{1}{m-1}\partial_z \Phi,
\]
so that the foregoing expression becomes
\begin{multline*}
= \frac{1}{(m-1)^3}\{-(8m-16)H^2 d\Phi + \nu^2 dH \nabla H\} \\
- \frac{(3m-6)(3m-7)}{(m-1)^2}\bigl\{\tfrac{6m-14}{m-1}H^2 \partial \Phi
- \tfrac{3m-7}{m-1}\Phi \partial H\bigr\} \\
+ \frac{1}{(m-1)^2}\{-(8m-16)H^2 \partial H + (m-1)\partial H \nabla H\} \\
+ \frac{1}{(m-1)^2}\{2H(\partial . \nabla)H - \nu^2 H \nabla H\};
\end{multline*}
or finally
\begin{multline*}
\partial_x U \partial_x H + 2\partial_y U \partial_y H + 2\partial_z U \partial_z H = \\
\frac{1}{(m-1)^3}\{(-6m^2 + 18m - 12)H^2 \partial \Phi + (-17m^2 + 60m - 55)H^2 \Phi \partial H\} \\
+ \frac{1}{(m-1)^3} \nu \{2(m-2)H^2(\partial . \nabla)H + (8m-16)H dH \nabla H\} \\
+ \frac{1}{(m-1)^3}\nu^2 \{-H^2 \partial \Omega\}.
\end{multline*}

\begin{art}
\textbf{Calculation of $\partial_x^2 U \partial_x^2 U$.}

This is
\[
\frac{1}{(m-1)^4}H \partial H.
\]
\end{art}

\subsection*{Article Nos.\ 34 and 35.---The Jacobian Formula.}

\setcounter{art}{33}
\begin{art}
In general, if $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$ be functions of the degrees $p$, $q$, $r$, $s$ respectively,
we have identically
\[
\begin{vmatrix}
pP, & qQ, & rR, & sS \\
\partial_x P, & \partial_x Q, & \partial_x R, & \partial_x S \\
\partial_y P, & \partial_y Q, & \partial_y R, & \partial_y S \\
\partial_z P, & \partial_z Q, & \partial_z R, & \partial_z S
\end{vmatrix}
= 0,
\]
or, what is the same thing,
\[
pP \Jac(Q, R, S) - qQ \Jac(R, S, P) + rR \Jac(S, P, Q) - sS \Jac(P, Q, R) = 0.
\]
\end{art}

\setcounter{art}{34}
\begin{art}
Hence in particular if $P=U$, and assuming $U^m = 0$, we have
\[
- qQ \Jac(R, S, U) + rR \Jac(S, U, Q) - sS \Jac(U, Q, R) = 0.
\]
If moreover $Q = S^2$, and therefore $s = 1$, we have
\[
- S^2 \Jac(R, S, U) + rR \Jac(S, U, Q) - sS \Jac(U, S^2, R) = 0;
\]
or, as this may also be written,
\[
- S^2 \Jac(U, R, S) + rR \Jac(U, R, S) - sS \Jac(U, S^2, R) = 0;
\]
that is
\[
-rR \Jac(U, R, S) + rR dS - sS dR = 0.
\]
\end{art}

\begin{art}
Particular cases are
\begin{align}
&(2m-4)\Phi \partial H - (3m-6)H \partial \Phi = \tfrac{3}{m-2}\Jac(U, \Phi, H),
&&\text{ante, No.\ 12}, \\
&(5m-11)\nabla H \partial H - (3m-6)H \partial(\nabla H)
= \tfrac{3}{m-2}\Jac(U, \nabla H, H),
&&\text{''} \\
&(2m-4)\nabla \partial H - (3m-6)H \partial \nabla = \tfrac{3}{m-2}\Jac(U, \nabla, H),
&&\text{''} \\
&(5m-12)\Omega \partial H - (3m-6)H \partial \Omega
= \tfrac{3}{m-2}\Jac(U, \Omega, H),
&&\text{No.\ 18}, \\
&(8m-18)\Psi \partial H - (3m-6)H \partial \Psi
= \tfrac{3}{m-2}\Jac(U, \Psi, H),
&&\text{No.\ 19}, \\
&(2m-4)\Omega \partial H - (3m-6)H \Omega \partial
= \tfrac{3}{m-2}\Jac(U, \Omega_\Phi, H),
&&\text{No.\ 25}, \\
&(3m-8)\Omega \partial H - (3m-6)H \Omega \partial
= \tfrac{3}{m-2}\Jac(U, \Omega_\Psi, H),
&&\text{''}
\end{align}
where it is to be observed that in the third of these formulae I have, in accordance
with the notation before employed, written $\partial . \nabla$ to denote the result of the operation
$\partial$ performed on $\nabla$ as operand. I have also written $\nabla : \partial H$ to show that the operation
$\nabla$ is not to be performed on the following $\partial H$ as an operand, but that it remains
as an unperformed operation. As regards the last two equations, it is to be remarked
that the demonstration in the last preceding number depends merely on the homo-
geneity of the functions, and the orders of these functions: in the former of the two
formul\ae, the differentiation of $\Omega$ is performed upon $\Omega$ in regard to the coordinates
$(x, y, z)$ in so far only as they enter through $U$, and $\Omega$ is therefore to be regarded
as a function of the order $2m-4$; in the latter of the two formul\ae\ the differentiation
is to be performed in regard to the coordinates in so far only as they enter through
$H$, and $\Omega$ is therefore to be regarded as a function of the order $3m-8$. The two
formul\ae\ might also be written
\begin{align*}
(2m-4)\nabla \partial H - (3m-6)H \partial \Omega_\Phi &= \tfrac{3}{m-2}\Jac(U, \Omega_\Phi, H), \\
(3m-8)\nabla \partial H - (3m-6)H \partial \Omega_\Psi &= \tfrac{3}{m-2}\Jac(U, \Omega_\Psi, H);
\end{align*}
and it may be noticed that, adding these together, we obtain the foregoing formula,
\[
(5m-12)\Omega \partial H - (3m-6)H \partial \Omega = \tfrac{3}{m-2}\Jac(U, \Omega, H).
\]
\end{art}

\subsection*{Article Nos.\ 36 to 40.---Proof of equation
$(\partial . \nabla)H = \Jac(U, H, \Phi)$, used in the second transformation.}

\setcounter{art}{35}
\begin{art}
We have
\begin{align*}
\nabla &= (\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} x, y, z \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z) \\
&= (\fA\partial_x + \fH\partial_y + \fG\partial_z,
\fH\partial_x + \fB\partial_y + \fF\partial_z,
\fG\partial_x + \fF\partial_y + \fC\partial_z \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \lambda, \mu, \nu).
\end{align*}
Also
\begin{align*}
\partial &= (B\nu - C\mu)\partial_x + (C\lambda - A\nu)\partial_y
+ (A\mu - B\lambda)\partial_z \\
&= \lambda P + \mu Q + \nu R,
\end{align*}
if for a moment $P, Q, R = C\partial_y - B\partial_z$, $A\partial_z - C\partial_x$,
$B\partial_x - A\partial_y$.
Hence
\[
\partial . \nabla = (\lambda P + \mu Q + \nu R).
(\fA\partial_x + \fH\partial_y + \fG\partial_z,
\fH\partial_x + \fB\partial_y + \fF\partial_z,
\fG\partial_x + \fF\partial_y + \fC\partial_z \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \lambda, \mu, \nu),
\]
viz. coefficient of $\lambda^2$
\[
= P\fA\partial_x + P\fH\partial_y + P\fG\partial_z
\]
and so for the other terms; whence also in $(\partial . \nabla)H$ the coefficients of
$\lambda^2$, \&c.\ are
\[
(P\fA\partial_x + P\fH\partial_y + P\fG\partial_z)H, \text{ \&c.}
\]
\end{art}

\setcounter{art}{36}
\begin{art}
Again, in $\Jac(U, H, \Phi)$, where $\Phi = (\fA, \fB, \fC, \fF, \fG, \fH \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \lambda, \mu, \nu)^2$,
the coefficients of $\lambda^2$, \&c.\ are $\Jac(U, H, \fA)$, \&c.; and hence the assumed equation
\[
(\partial . \nabla)H = \Jac(U, H, \Phi),
\]
in regard to the term in $\lambda^2$, is
\[
(P\fA\partial_x + P\fH\partial_y + P\fG\partial_z)H = \Jac(U, H, \fA),
\]
and we have
\begin{align*}
\Jac(U, H, \fA) &=
\begin{vmatrix}
A, & B, & C \\
\partial_x H, & \partial_y H, & \partial_z H \\
\partial_x, & \partial_y, & \partial_z
\end{vmatrix}
\fA \\
&= \{\partial_x H(C\partial_z - B\partial_y) + \partial_y H(A\partial_z - C\partial_x)
+ \partial_z H(B\partial_y - A\partial_x)\}\fA \\
&= (\partial_x H \cdot P + \partial_y H \cdot Q + \partial_z H \cdot R)\fA;
\end{align*}
so that the equation is
\[
P\fA\partial_x H + P\fH\partial_y H + P\fG\partial_z H
= P\fA\partial_x H + Q\fA\partial_y H + R\fA\partial_z H,
\]
or, as this may be written,
\begin{multline*}
[(B\partial_z - C\partial_y)\fA - (C\partial_z - A\partial_x)\fA]\partial_y H \\
+ [(B\partial_z - C\partial_y)\fG - (A\partial_y - B\partial_x)\fA]\partial_z H = 0.
\end{multline*}
\end{art}

\setcounter{art}{37}
\begin{art}
The coefficient of $\partial_y H$ is
\[
B(\fA\partial_z - \fG\partial_x) - C(\fA\partial_y - \fH\partial_x),
\]
which, in virtue of the identity, post. No.\ 40,
$3a\fA + 3b\fB + 3c\fC = 0$,
\[
= \fA\partial_x \fA + \fB\partial_y \fA + \fC\partial_z \fA;
\]
and in like manner the coefficient of $\partial_z H$ is
\[
= -(A\partial_y \fA + B\partial_y \fB + C\partial_y \fC),
\]
so that the equation is
\[
(\fA\partial_x \fA + \fB\partial_y \fA + \fC\partial_z \fA)\partial_y H
- (A\partial_y \fA + B\partial_y \fB + C\partial_y \fC)\partial_z H = 0.
\]
\end{art}

\setcounter{art}{38}
\begin{art}
But we have
\begin{align*}
\fA a + \fH h + \fG g &= H, \\
\fA h + \fB b + \fF f &= 0, \\
\fA g + \fF f + \fC c &= 0,
\end{align*}
or multiplying by $x$, $y$, $z$ and adding,
\[
(m-1)(\fA A + \fB B + \fC C) = xH;
\]
whence also
\begin{align*}
(m-1)(\fA \partial_x A + \fB \partial_x B + \fC \partial_x C) &= x\partial_x H, \\
\intertext{that is}
(m-1)(\fA \partial_x \fA + \fB \partial_y \fA + \fC \partial_z \fA) &= x\partial_x H; \\
\intertext{and in like manner}
(m-1)(A \partial_y \fA + B \partial_y \fB + C \partial_y \fC) &= x\partial_y H, \\
(m-1)(A \partial_z \fA + B \partial_z \fB + C \partial_z \fC) &= x\partial_z H,
\end{align*}
whence the equation in question. The terms in $\lambda^2$ are thus shown to be equal, and
it might in a similar manner be shown that the terms in $\mu\nu$ are equal; the other
terms will then be equal, and we have therefore
\[
(\partial . \nabla)H = \Jac(U, H, \Phi).
\]
\end{art}

\setcounter{art}{39}
\begin{art}
The identity
\[
\partial_x \fA + \partial_y \fB + \partial_z \fC = 0
\]
assumed in the course of the foregoing proof is easily proved. We have in fact
\begin{align*}
\partial_x \fA + \partial_y \fB + \partial_z \fC
&= \partial_x(bc-f^2) + \partial_y(fg-ch) + \partial_z(fh-bg) \\
&= b(\partial_x c - \partial_y f) + c(\partial_x b - \partial_z h)
+ f(-2\partial_x f + \partial_y g + \partial_z h) \\
&\quad + g(\partial_y f - \partial_z b) + h(-\partial_y c + \partial_z f),
\end{align*}
where the coefficients of $b$, $c$, $f$, $g$, $h$ separately vanish: we have of course the system
\begin{align*}
\partial_x \fA + \partial_y \fH + \partial_z \fG &= 0, \\
\partial_x \fH + \partial_y \fB + \partial_z \fF &= 0, \\
\partial_x \fG + \partial_y \fF + \partial_z \fC &= 0.
\end{align*}
\end{art}

\subsection*{Article Nos.\ 41 to 46.---Proof of identities for the fourth transformation.}

\setcounter{art}{40}
\begin{art}
Consider the coefficients $(a, b, c, f, g, h)$ and the inverse set
$(\fA, \fB, \fC, \fF, \fG, \fH)$, and the coefficients $(a', b', c', f', g', h')$, and the inverse set
$(\fApr, \fBpr, \fCpr, \fFpr, \fGpr, \fHpr)$; then we have identically
\begin{multline*}
(a, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} x, y, z)^2 (\fApr, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a, \dots)
- (\fApr, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} ax + hy + gz, \dots)^2 \\
= (a', \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} x, y, z)^2 (\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a', \dots)
- (\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a'x + h'y + g'z, \dots)^2,
\end{multline*}
where $(\fApr, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a, \dots)$ and $(\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a', \dots)$ stand for
$(\fApr, \fBpr, \fCpr, \fFpr, \fGpr, \fHpr \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a, b, c, 2f, 2g, 2h)$ and
$(\fA, \fB, \fC, \fF, \fG, \fH \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a', b', c', 2f', 2g', 2h')$
respectively.
\end{art}

\setcounter{art}{41}
\begin{art}
Taking $(a, b, c, f, g, h)$, the second differential coefficients of a function $U$
of the order $m$, and in like manner $(a', b', c', f', g', h')$, the second differential coefficients
of a function $U'$ of the order $m'$, we have
\begin{multline*}
m(m-1)U \cdot (\fApr, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2 H
- (m-1)^2 (\fApr, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial_x U, \partial_y U, \partial_z U)^2 \\
= m'(m'-1)U' \cdot (\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2 H
- (m'-1)^2 (\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial_x U', \partial_y U', \partial_z U');
\end{multline*}
and in particular if $U'$ be the Hessian of $U$, then $m' = 3m - 6$.
\end{art}

\setcounter{art}{42}
\begin{art}
Hence writing
\[
\Omega_1 = (\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2 H, \quad
\Omega_2 = (\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial_x H, \partial_y H, \partial_z H)^2,
\]
\[
\Omega'_1 = (\fApr, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)^2 U, \quad
\Omega'_2 = (\fApr, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial_x U, \partial_y U, \partial_z U)^2,
\]
we have
\[
m(m-1)U \Omega_2 - (m-1)^2 \Omega'_2 = (3m-6)(3m-7)H \Omega_1 - (3m-7)^2 \Omega'_1;
\]
or if $U = 0$, then
\[
-(m-1)^2 \Omega'_2 = (3m-6)(3m-7)H \Omega_1 - (3m-7)^2 \Omega'_1;
\]
whence also
\[
-(m-1)^2 \partial \Omega'_2 = (3m-6)(3m-7)\{H \partial \Omega_1 + \Omega_1 \partial H\}
- (3m-7)^2 \partial \Omega'_1,
\]
which is the formula, ante No.\ 21.
\end{art}

\setcounter{art}{43}
\begin{art}
Recurring to the original formula, since this is an actual identity, we may
operate on it with the differential symbol $\partial$ on the three assumptions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
\item $(a, b, c, f, g, h)$, $(\fA, \fB, \fC, \fF, \fG, \fH)$ are alone variable.
\item $(a', b', c', f', g', h')$, $(\fApr, \fBpr, \fCpr, \fFpr, \fGpr, \fHpr)$ are alone variable.
\item $(x, y, z)$ are alone variable.
\end{enumerate}
\end{art}

\setcounter{art}{44}
\begin{art}
If in these equations respectively we suppose as before that $(a, b, c, f, g, h)$
are the second differential coefficients of a function $U$ of the order $m$, and
$(a', b', c', f', g', h')$ the second differential coefficients of a function $V$ of the order $m'$;
and that $(A, B, C)$, $(A', B', C')$ are the first differential coefficients of these functions
respectively, then after some easy reductions we have
\begin{align*}
&= (a', \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} x, y, z \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial_x, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a, \dots) \\
&\quad - (a', \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a'x + h'y + g'z, \dots)^2, \\
&= (\partial a', \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} x, y, z \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a', \dots) \\
&\quad + (a', \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} x, y, z \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial a', \dots) \\
&\quad - 2(\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a'x + h'y + g'z, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} x\partial a' + y\partial h' + z\partial g', \dots), \\
&= 2(a', \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} x, y, z \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial_x, \partial_y, \partial_z)(\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a', \dots) \\
&\quad - 2(\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a'x + h'y + g'z, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a'\partial_x + h'\partial_y + g'\partial_z, \dots).
\end{align*}
\begin{multline*}
(m-1)(m-2)\partial U (\fApr, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a, \dots)
+ m(m-1)U(\fApr, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial a, \dots) \\
- 2(m-1)(m-2)(\fApr, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} A, B, C \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \partial A, \partial B, \partial C)
\end{multline*}
\begin{multline*}
m(m-1)U(\partial A', \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} \fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a', \dots)
- (m-1)^2(\partial A', \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} A, B, C)^2 \\
= m'(m'-1)U'(a\fA, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} a', \dots)
- (m'-1)^2(\fB, \dots \mathbin{\mathfrak{q}} A', B', C)^2
\end{multline*}
\end{art}
